questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with regular 28-day menstrual cycles comes to the clinic for preconception counseling. She asks how many days before ovulation intercourse can still result in pregnancy. Based on the survival of gametes in the female reproductive tract, which of the following is the most accurate answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 day

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: 7 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: 10 days

explanation.summary: Sperm survive 3 to 5 days in the female reproductive tract, so intercourse up to 5 days before ovulation can produce a pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fertilization must occur within about 24 hours of ovulation, but sperm can live for three to five days in the reproductive tract. Pregnancy is therefore possible from intercourse up to five days before ovulation, although the chance is highest within 24 hours of ovulation and the day before.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One day describes the window during which the ovulated egg remains fertilizable, not the limit of sperm survival before ovulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two days is within the fertile window but understates it; sperm survival extends the window to about five days.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seven days exceeds the maximum sperm survival of three to five days in the reproductive tract.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ten days far exceeds sperm survival; conception from intercourse this early is not possible.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman undergoing fertility treatment has an oocyte retrieved from the fallopian tube shortly after ovulation, before any exposure to sperm. Examination of the cell's nuclear contents would show it arrested at which of the following stages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prophase of meiosis I

choices.label: B
choices.text: Metaphase of meiosis I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anaphase of meiosis I

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metaphase of meiosis II

choices.label: E
choices.text: Telophase of meiosis II

explanation.summary: The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase of meiosis II and completes meiosis II only if fertilization occurs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The LH surge drives the primary oocyte to complete meiosis I, producing a secondary oocyte and the first polar body. The secondary oocyte enters meiosis II but arrests at metaphase II, and it remains there at ovulation until sperm penetration triggers completion of meiosis II with extrusion of the second polar body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prophase I is where the primary oocyte is arrested from fetal life until the LH surge at puberty, before ovulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Meiosis I is completed under the influence of the LH surge before ovulation, so the released cell has passed metaphase I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anaphase I occurs during completion of meiosis I prior to ovulation; the released cell has already finished this division.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Telophase II occurs only after fertilization triggers completion of meiosis II; an unfertilized oocyte never reaches it.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman gives birth to an infant with hypotonia and characteristic facial features. Karyotype of the infant shows 47,XX,+21, and studies indicate the extra chromosome is maternal in origin. Which of the following age-related changes in the mother's oocytes most likely predisposed to this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of crossing over during prophase I

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decline in chromatid cohesion and spindle integrity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Accumulated replication errors from repeated mitoses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premature completion of meiosis II before ovulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of cortical granules from the oocyte cortex

explanation.summary: Prolonged meiotic arrest in aging oocytes degrades cohesion and spindle integrity, predisposing to nondisjunction and trisomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Female meiosis begins in fetal life and remains arrested for decades. With increasing maternal age, cohesion between chromatids and spindle integrity decline, predisposing to nondisjunction, most commonly during meiosis I but also during meiosis II. Fertilization of the resulting egg carrying an extra chromosome 21 by a normal haploid sperm produces trisomy 21.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crossing over in prophase I generates genetic diversity; its failure is not the described mechanism of age-related aneuploidy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cumulative replication errors from ongoing mitotic divisions describe the paternal-age effect in spermatogenesis, producing de novo mutations rather than maternal trisomy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meiosis II in the oocyte completes only after fertilization; it does not finish prematurely before ovulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortical granules prevent polyspermy after fertilization; their loss would not cause a maternally derived extra chromosome.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man and his 30-year-old partner have a child diagnosed with an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a de novo point mutation shown to be of paternal origin. Which of the following features of spermatogenesis best explains the association between advanced paternal age and this type of mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prolonged meiotic arrest of primary spermatocytes over decades

choices.label: B
choices.text: Numerous mitotic divisions of spermatogonia with repeated DNA replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progressive loss of cohesion between sister chromatids with age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incomplete capacitation of sperm in the female reproductive tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exposure of sperm to the acidic environment of the vagina

explanation.summary: Continuous spermatogonial mitoses throughout adult life accumulate DNA replication errors, making sperm a major source of de novo mutations with advancing paternal age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spermatogenesis involves continuous cell division throughout adult life, with spermatogonia undergoing numerous mitotic divisions before entering meiosis. Each round of DNA replication carries a risk of error, so the mutation burden rises with paternal age, making spermatogenesis a significant source of de novo mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prolonged meiotic arrest is a feature of oogenesis, not spermatogenesis; spermatocytes begin meiosis at puberty and complete it in the testes without decades-long arrest.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Age-related decline in cohesion and spindle integrity is the maternal mechanism predisposing to aneuploidy, not point mutations of paternal origin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Capacitation affects a sperm's ability to fertilize the egg; it does not alter the DNA sequence carried by the sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal acidity kills sperm outright; it is a barrier to fertilization, not a cause of heritable point mutations.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea and new right lower quadrant pain. A serum human chorionic gonadotropin test is positive, and transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine pregnancy but reveals a right adnexal mass. The abnormally implanted tissue is most likely located in which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Graafian follicle of the ovary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cervical canal of the uterus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ampulla of the fallopian tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interstitial uterotubal junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peritoneal cavity of the pelvis

explanation.summary: Ectopic pregnancy most often implants in the fallopian tube, specifically the ampulla, the usual site of fertilization.
explanation.whyCorrect: The egg normally meets the sperm in the ampulla, in the distal third of the fallopian tube. When the fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, the most common location is the fallopian tube, specifically the ampulla. Diagnosis uses an hCG blood test to confirm pregnancy and ultrasound to determine location, and the ectopic tissue must be removed medically or surgically because tubal rupture and bleeding are life-threatening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ovary releases the oocyte but is not the most common site of ectopic implantation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical implantation is not the typical location; the cervix acts mainly as a barrier to ascending sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The uterotubal junction is a selective barrier for sperm transit, not the most common ectopic site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abdominal (peritoneal) implantation occurs but is far less common than implantation in the ampulla.

questions.stem: In an assisted reproduction laboratory, freshly ejaculated sperm placed directly with mature oocytes fail to fertilize them, whereas sperm first incubated in medium that mimics female reproductive tract secretions succeed. The change induced by this incubation is best characterized by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Release of hydrolytic enzymes from the acrosomal cap

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of sperm surface antigens with activation of tail motility

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exocytosis of cortical granules at the cell membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fusion of the sperm membrane with the oocyte membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extrusion of a polar body from the cell

explanation.summary: Capacitation is a biochemical change during transit that strips surface antigens, activates the tail, and primes the acrosome via rising calcium and cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: During transit through the female tract, in part through interaction with cervical secretions, sperm undergo capacitation. They lose surface antigens, which facilitates binding to the egg, and their motility increases through tail activation. A gradual increase in intracellular calcium enhances cAMP generation, priming the sperm for the acrosome reaction; only capacitated sperm can fertilize an ovum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acrosomal enzyme release is the acrosome reaction, a later event at the zona pellucida for which capacitation merely primes the sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortical granule exocytosis is the ovum's response to fertilization that prevents polyspermy, not a change in sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane fusion occurs at the oolemma after the sperm has penetrated the egg's outer layers, downstream of capacitation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polar body extrusion is a feature of oocyte meiosis, not of sperm maturation.

questions.stem: During fertilization, hundreds of capacitated sperm bind to receptors in the zona pellucida of an ovulated oocyte. Which of the following events most directly enables a bound sperm to traverse this glycoprotein layer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Release of acrosin and other hydrolytic enzymes from the sperm head

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exocytosis of lysosomal enzymes from cortical granules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binding of fertilin to integrin on the oocyte membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Buffering of the local environment by alkaline semen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ciliary currents generated by the fallopian tube epithelium

explanation.summary: The acrosome reaction releases hydrolytic enzymes such as acrosin that, with sperm motility, allow penetration of the zona pellucida.
explanation.whyCorrect: After binding to zona pellucida receptors, a calcium surge within the sperm triggers the acrosome reaction. The released hydrolytic enzymes, including acrosin, degrade the egg's layers and, together with exposed sperm-surface proteins and sperm motility, create a tunnel through which the head, neck, and middle piece enter the egg.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortical granule exocytosis comes from the ovum after fertilization and blocks additional sperm; it does not help sperm penetrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fertilin-integrin binding mediates fusion at the oocyte plasma membrane after the zona has already been crossed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alkaline semen buffers vaginal acidity early in transit; it plays no role at the zona pellucida.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ciliary movement propels the ovum and later the zygote along the tube; it does not carry sperm through the zona.

questions.stem: A fertilization study examines a zygote that arrested early in development and is found to contain one maternal and two paternal chromosome complements along with an abnormal centrosome number. Failure of which of the following processes most likely allowed this abnormality to occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium-triggered exocytosis of cortical granules by the ovum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium-triggered release of acrosomal enzymes by the sperm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Capacitation of sperm during transit through the tract

choices.label: D
choices.text: Completion of meiosis II by the fertilized oocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Segregation of sister chromatids during meiosis II

explanation.summary: The cortical reaction, triggered by a rise in intracellular calcium in the ovum, blocks polyspermy; its failure permits a second sperm to enter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two paternal chromosome sets with an abnormal centrosome complement indicate polyspermy, which usually prevents viable zygote development. Normally, fertilization by one sperm raises intracellular calcium in the ovum and triggers the cortical reaction: cortical granules release lysosomal enzymes that make the plasma membrane impenetrable and alter the zona pellucida so no additional sperm can bind.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The acrosome reaction enables the first sperm to penetrate; its failure would prevent fertilization, not cause dispermy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed capacitation would leave sperm unable to fertilize at all, producing no zygote rather than a dispermic one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure to complete meiosis II would alter the maternal contribution, not add an extra paternal chromosome set.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A meiosis II segregation error causes trisomy of a single chromosome, not an entire extra paternal genome with extra centrosomes.

questions.stem: Shortly after ovulation, a released oocyte is captured by the fimbriae of the fallopian tube. The outermost cellular layer surrounding the oocyte contributes most directly to this capture through which of the following properties?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adhesion molecules on retained granulosa cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycoprotein receptors that bind capacitated sperm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysosomal enzymes stored in cortical granules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrin receptors on the plasma membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cilia that beat toward the uterine cavity

explanation.summary: The corona radiata consists of granulosa cells rich in adhesion molecules that help the fimbriae capture the ovum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The corona radiata is made of follicular (granulosa) cells that formed around the developing oocyte and remain attached when the egg is released. These cells are rich in adhesion molecules that help the ovum be captured by the fimbriae of the fallopian tube, and the corona is also the first layer sperm must penetrate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sperm-binding glycoprotein receptors belong to the zona pellucida, the layer deep to the corona radiata, and serve fertilization rather than capture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortical granules lie beneath the oocyte plasma membrane and act after fertilization to prevent polyspermy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Integrin is the receptor on the oocyte plasma membrane that binds sperm fertilin; it does not mediate fimbrial capture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cilia belong to the fallopian tube lining, not to the cell layers of the ovum.

questions.stem: During in vitro studies of fertilization, a sperm that has passed through the corona radiata and zona pellucida reaches the oocyte plasma membrane. Interaction between which of the following pairs of molecules most directly mediates binding and fusion of the two cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acrosin on the sperm and glycoproteins of the zona pellucida

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fertilin on the sperm head and integrin on the oocyte membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surface antigens on the sperm and phagocyte receptors in the uterus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adhesion molecules on granulosa cells and receptors on the fimbriae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cortical granule enzymes and receptors on the sperm midpiece

explanation.summary: Fertilin on the sperm head binds integrin on the oocyte plasma membrane to mediate sperm-egg binding and membrane fusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm and ovum bind with the help of surface proteins on both cells: fertilin is a protein on the head of the spermatozoon, and integrin is its receptor on the oocyte plasma membrane. Both facilitate binding and fusion of the plasma membranes, after which the sperm's head, neck, and middle piece enter the egg and release its genetic material.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acrosin is a hydrolytic acrosomal enzyme that degrades the zona pellucida; it acts before the sperm reaches the plasma membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Uterine phagocytes destroy sperm during transit; this interaction eliminates sperm rather than mediating fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adhesion molecules of the corona radiata help the fimbriae capture the ovum, not bind sperm to the oolemma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortical granule enzymes act after fertilization to make the membrane impenetrable; they do not mediate sperm binding.

questions.stem: A cell biologist analyzes the gamete released from a woman's ovary at ovulation, before any contact with sperm. Which of the following best describes the chromosome number and DNA content of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 46 chromosomes, 4C DNA content

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46 chromosomes, 2C DNA content

choices.label: C
choices.text: 23 chromosomes, 2C DNA content

choices.label: D
choices.text: 23 chromosomes, 1C DNA content

choices.label: E
choices.text: 92 chromosomes, 4C DNA content

explanation.summary: The ovulated secondary oocyte is haploid with duplicated chromatids: 23 chromosomes (1N) and 2C DNA content.
explanation.whyCorrect: The LH surge drives completion of meiosis I, which separates homologous chromosomes and produces a secondary oocyte (1N, 2C) plus the first polar body. This secondary oocyte arrests at metaphase II and is the cell released at ovulation; it reaches 1N, 1C only after fertilization triggers completion of meiosis II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 46 chromosomes with 4C content describes the primary oocyte after S phase, arrested in meiosis I before the LH surge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 46 chromosomes with 2C content describes a diploid cell such as an oogonium before DNA replication, not the ovulated gamete.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 23 chromosomes with 1C content describes the mature ovum, which forms only after fertilization completes meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 92 chromosomes never occur in normal gametogenesis; DNA replication doubles content to 4C without doubling the chromosome count to 92.

questions.stem: Of the millions of sperm deposited in the female reproductive tract during intercourse, only a tiny number reach the site of fertilization. The largest proportion of sperm is destroyed shortly after ejaculation by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acidity of the vaginal environment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phagocytes residing in the uterine cavity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mechanical obstruction at the uterotubal junction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enzymes released during the cortical reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydrolytic enzymes within the zona pellucida

explanation.summary: The acidic vaginal environment kills the majority of sperm shortly after ejaculation, forming the first major barrier to fertilization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many of the millions of sperm entering the vagina are rapidly destroyed by its acidic environment, and only a small fraction passes through the cervix. Alkaline components of semen and cervical mucus buffer the acid, providing temporary protection so some sperm can transit into the uterus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Uterine phagocytes destroy sperm later in transit, after most have already been killed in the vagina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The uterotubal junction is a major selective barrier, but it acts on the small population that survives the vagina, cervix, and uterus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cortical reaction occurs in the ovum after fertilization to block polyspermy; it does not destroy sperm in transit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The zona pellucida selects and binds sperm at the egg itself; it is not responsible for the massive early loss of sperm.

questions.stem: Analysis of the four haploid gametes derived from a single germ cell shows that each carries a chromosome 7 containing segments from both the maternal and the paternal homolog. The exchange of genetic material that produced these recombinant chromosomes occurred during which of the following stages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Metaphase of meiosis I

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prophase of meiosis I

choices.label: C
choices.text: S phase preceding meiosis I

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anaphase of meiosis II

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prophase of meiosis II

explanation.summary: Crossing over occurs during prophase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosomes pair and exchange genetic material.
explanation.whyCorrect: Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells, ensuring genetic diversity. The recombination responsible for that diversity is crossing over, which occurs during prophase of meiosis I when homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At metaphase I the paired homologs align for separation; the exchange of segments has already taken place in prophase I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S phase replicates DNA to produce the 4C primary germ cell; it copies chromosomes rather than exchanging material between homologs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anaphase of meiosis II separates sister chromatids; homologs are no longer paired and no exchange occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: By prophase II the homologs have already been separated in meiosis I, so no pairing or exchange between them is possible.

questions.stem: Histologic examination of the ovary of a full-term female infant shows numerous oocytes, each surrounded by a single flattened layer of granulosa cells. Nuclear analysis of one of these oocytes would show which of the following chromosome numbers and DNA contents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 23 chromosomes, 1C DNA content

choices.label: B
choices.text: 23 chromosomes, 2C DNA content

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46 chromosomes, 2C DNA content

choices.label: D
choices.text: 46 chromosomes, 4C DNA content

choices.label: E
choices.text: 92 chromosomes, 4C DNA content

explanation.summary: The oocyte of a primordial follicle is a primary oocyte arrested in meiosis I, with 46 chromosomes and 4C DNA content.
explanation.whyCorrect: An oocyte surrounded by a single flattened layer of granulosa cells defines a primordial follicle, and its oocyte is a primary oocyte arrested in the first meiotic division. Because DNA replicated in S phase before the arrest, the primary oocyte is 2N with 4C DNA content, that is, 46 chromosomes with doubled DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 23 chromosomes with 1C content describes the mature haploid ovum, which forms only after fertilization completes meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 23 chromosomes with 2C content describes the secondary oocyte produced when meiosis I is completed at puberty, not the arrested oocyte of an infant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 46 chromosomes with 2C content describes an oogonium before DNA replication; the oocyte of a primordial follicle has already replicated its DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 92 chromosomes never occur in gametogenesis; replication doubles DNA content to 4C without doubling the chromosome count.

questions.stem: During gametogenesis, a germ cell completes meiosis I, and its daughter cells proceed directly into meiosis II. Which of the following features distinguishes meiosis II from meiosis I?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It proceeds without a preceding round of DNA replication

choices.label: B
choices.text: It separates homologous chromosome pairs from each other

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is preceded by crossing over between paired homologs

choices.label: D
choices.text: It doubles the DNA content of the dividing cell to 4C

choices.label: E
choices.text: It produces two diploid daughter cells from each dividing cell

explanation.summary: Meiosis II is a division without an intervening round of DNA replication, yielding haploid gametes with 23 chromosomes each.
explanation.whyCorrect: Before meiosis I, DNA replicates in S phase to produce a 46-chromosome, 2N, 4C primary germ cell. In meiosis II the cells divide again without replication, producing four daughter cells, each with a single set of 23 chromosomes; these are the haploid gametes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Separation of homologous chromosomes is the defining event of meiosis I, not meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crossing over occurs during prophase I, before meiosis I completes; it does not precede meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DNA content is doubled to 4C by S phase before meiosis I; no replication occurs before meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Meiosis II yields haploid (1N) cells; diploid daughter cells are a product of mitosis, not the second meiotic division.

questions.stem: A study quantifies oogonia in human ovarian tissue sampled across the lifespan. The number of oogonia is greatest at which of the following times?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the beginning of the first trimester

choices.label: B
choices.text: At birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: By mid-gestation of fetal life

choices.label: D
choices.text: At puberty

choices.label: E
choices.text: At the time of each ovulation

explanation.summary: Oogonia, formed by mitosis of primitive germ cells beginning in the first trimester, reach their peak number in the fetus by mid-gestation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oogenesis begins in the female fetus during the first trimester, when primitive germ cells undergo mitosis to form oogonia. A peak number of oogonia are present in the fetus by mid-gestation; thereafter, oocytes arrest in meiosis I as primary oocytes and most follicles undergo atresia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oogenesis is only beginning in the first trimester; the mitotic expansion of oogonia has not yet reached its peak.
whyWrongByChoice.B: By birth the peak has passed; the population has already declined from its mid-gestational maximum as follicles degenerate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: By puberty the ovary contains arrested primary oocytes in follicles, far fewer than the mid-gestational peak of oogonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte during reproductive life, long after the oogonial population peaked in the fetus.

questions.stem: In the fetal ovary, primary oocytes become surrounded by a single flattened layer of granulosa cells, forming primordial follicles. Which of the following describes the fate of most of these primordial follicles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are released at ovulation over the reproductive years

choices.label: B
choices.text: They mature fully and are stored until menopause

choices.label: C
choices.text: They complete meiosis and persist as haploid ova

choices.label: D
choices.text: They transform directly into layers of granulosa cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: They degenerate and are resorbed before reaching maturity

explanation.summary: Most primordial follicles undergo atresia, degenerating and being resorbed before they reach maturity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although a peak number of oogonia are present by mid-gestation and many become primary oocytes within primordial follicles, most of these primordial follicles undergo atresia, a process of degeneration and resorption, before they ever mature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only a small minority of follicles ever reach ovulation; the majority are lost to atresia long before.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicles do not mature fully and wait in storage; most degenerate without maturing at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meiosis remains arrested in primary oocytes; completion requires the LH surge and, for meiosis II, fertilization, which most follicles never reach.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulosa cells surround the oocyte to form the follicle; the oocyte itself does not convert into granulosa cells.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is at midcycle of a regular menstrual cycle. Serum studies show a marked rise in gonadotropins, and one day later a follicle releases a secondary oocyte. Which of the following most directly stimulated the primary oocyte to resume and complete meiosis I?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Positive-feedback rise in estradiol from granulosa cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: The surge of luteinizing hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sustained rise in follicle-stimulating hormone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of human chorionic gonadotropin

choices.label: E
choices.text: A midcycle fall in progesterone

explanation.summary: The LH surge is the direct stimulus for the primary oocyte to resume and complete meiosis I, producing a secondary oocyte and the first polar body.
explanation.whyCorrect: At puberty, increasing titers of LH and FSH prompt granulosa cells to produce high levels of estrogen, and the LH surge then stimulates the arrested primary oocyte to resume and complete meiosis I. The result is a secondary oocyte (1N, 2C) and the first polar body, followed by arrest at metaphase II and release at ovulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol drives the positive feedback that produces the LH surge, but it is not the direct trigger of meiotic resumption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FSH supports follicular granulosa cell function and estrogen production; it is not the surge that reactivates meiosis I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: hCG is the hormone detected by pregnancy testing after conception; it plays no role in triggering ovulatory meiotic resumption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A fall in progesterone is not the described trigger; the lecture attributes meiotic resumption to the LH surge.

questions.stem: An infant is born with trisomy 21. Molecular studies show that the extra chromosome 21 is maternal in origin and that the error occurred during meiosis II of the oocyte. Failure of which of the following events produced the abnormal egg?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Separation of homologous chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pairing and crossing over between homologs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replication of DNA before the first division

choices.label: D
choices.text: Segregation of sister chromatids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extrusion of the first polar body

explanation.summary: A meiosis II error causing trisomy reflects failed segregation of sister chromatids, giving the egg an extra copy of one chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, whereas meiosis II segregates sister chromatids. An error in the segregation of sister chromatids during meiosis II leaves the egg with an extra copy of a chromosome; when this abnormal egg combines with a normal haploid sperm, the zygote carries three copies of that chromosome, producing a trisomy such as Down syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of homolog separation is a meiosis I error; the studies localized this error to meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crossing over in prophase I generates diversity; its failure does not add an extra chromosome copy in meiosis II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A replication problem would alter DNA content before meiosis I; it is not the segregation error of the second division.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The first polar body is extruded at completion of meiosis I; its extrusion is not the meiosis II event that failed.

questions.stem: During gametogenesis, one primary spermatocyte ultimately yields four sperm, whereas one primary oocyte yields only a single mature haploid ovum. Which of the following describes the fate of the other chromosomal complements generated by female meiosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are extruded as polar bodies that degenerate

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are retained in the ovum as accessory pronuclei

choices.label: C
choices.text: They develop into additional fertilizable ova

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are incorporated into the surrounding granulosa cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: They persist in the follicle as arrested oogonia

explanation.summary: Female meiosis discards the extra chromosomal complements as polar bodies, which degenerate, leaving a single haploid ovum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Completion of meiosis I produces a secondary oocyte and the first polar body, and completion of meiosis II after fertilization produces the mature haploid gamete and another polar body, which also degenerates. Unlike in males, where two cycles of meiosis produce four cells from one parent cell, meiosis in females produces a single haploid ovum.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The extra complements are extruded from the cell as polar bodies, not retained as additional pronuclei inside the ovum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only one functional ovum results from each primary oocyte; the polar bodies are not fertilizable eggs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulosa cells are follicular cells surrounding the oocyte; they do not absorb the discarded meiotic products.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oogonia are the mitotic precursors formed in fetal life; the products of oocyte meiosis are polar bodies, not oogonia.

questions.stem: Primary spermatocytes within the seminiferous tubules first begin to undergo meiosis I at which of the following times?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the first trimester of fetal life

choices.label: B
choices.text: By mid-gestation of fetal life

choices.label: C
choices.text: At birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: At puberty

choices.label: E
choices.text: After the fourth decade of life

explanation.summary: Male meiosis begins at puberty, when primary spermatocytes in the seminiferous tubules start meiosis I.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm development continues in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, where primary spermatocytes (2N, 4C) begin to undergo meiosis I at puberty. This contrasts with female gametogenesis, in which meiosis begins during fetal development and then arrests for decades.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Meiosis beginning in the first trimester describes oogenesis in the female fetus, not spermatogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mid-gestation is when the number of oogonia peaks in the female fetus; male meiosis has not begun at this stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: At birth the testes contain germ cells that have not yet entered meiosis; meiosis I awaits puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spermatogenesis continues throughout adult life, but meiosis begins at puberty, not in middle age.

questions.stem: In studies of sperm transit, millions of sperm are deposited in the vagina but only a tiny fraction reaches the fallopian tubes. Of the sperm that successfully traverse the cervix into the uterine cavity, many are eliminated before reaching the uterotubal junction. Which of the following is most responsible for this loss within the uterus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The acidic environment of the uterine cavity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trapping within alkaline cervical mucus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrolytic enzymes released from sperm acrosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Structural changes in the zona pellucida

choices.label: E
choices.text: Destruction by resident uterine phagocytes

explanation.summary: Sperm that penetrate the cervix and reach the uterus are further culled by resident uterine phagocytes before the survivors cross the uterotubal junction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once sperm penetrate the cervix and reach the uterus, more are destroyed by resident uterine phagocytes. The remaining sperm then cross the uterotubal junction, enter the fallopian tube, and swim upstream using their tails for locomotion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lethal acidic environment is the vagina's; it is not described as a property of the uterine cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical mucus, with alkaline semen, buffers vaginal acid and facilitates survival; it is not the agent of destruction inside the uterus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acrosomal enzymes are released at the egg to penetrate its layers; they do not destroy sperm during uterine transit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Zona pellucida changes occur after fertilization to block additional sperm at the egg, not in the uterine cavity.

questions.stem: Sperm that survive passage through the vagina, cervix, and uterine cavity must cross one final selective barrier before they can enter the fallopian tube and swim toward the egg. Which of the following structures constitutes this barrier?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cervical canal

choices.label: B
choices.text: The uterotubal junction

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fimbriated end of the tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: The zona pellucida

choices.label: E
choices.text: The corona radiata

explanation.summary: The uterotubal junction, the connection between the fallopian tube and the uterus, is the final major selective barrier sperm cross before entering the tube.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cervix and uterotubal junction are the major selective barriers of the tract. After surviving the vagina and uterine phagocytes, the remaining sperm cross the uterotubal junction, the connection point between the fallopian tube and the uterus, enter the tube, and swim upstream toward the ampulla.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cervical canal is an earlier barrier, already passed by the sperm described in this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fimbriae are at the ovarian end of the tube and capture the ovulated egg; sperm enter the tube from the uterine end.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The zona pellucida is a layer of the egg itself, encountered only after sperm reach the ovum in the ampulla.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The corona radiata surrounds the ovum; it is not part of the passage from the uterus into the tube.

questions.stem: Three days after fertilization in the ampulla, a dividing zygote is moving along the fallopian tube toward the uterine cavity. Which of the following forces most directly propels it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flagellar propulsion by the retained sperm tail

choices.label: B
choices.text: Swimming movements of the zygote itself

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beating of cilia lining the fallopian tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suction generated by the fimbriae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pressure of follicular fluid released at ovulation

explanation.summary: Cilia of the fallopian tube propel the ovum, and later the dividing zygote, down the tube toward the uterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The movement of cilia within the fallopian tube propels the ovum down the tube toward the uterus, and after fertilization the zygote migrates to the uterus by the same ciliary movement, implanting in the endometrium about a week later.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sperm tail does not enter the egg; only the head, neck, and middle piece do, so no flagellum propels the zygote.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The zygote has no motile apparatus of its own; it divides while being carried passively by the tube's cilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fimbriae act at ovulation to capture the released egg; they do not draw the zygote toward the uterus days later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Any fluid released at ovulation acts at the ovarian end at the time of release; it does not transport the zygote through the tube.

questions.stem: A woman conceives at midcycle, with fertilization occurring in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. Approximately how long after fertilization does the conceptus implant in the endometrium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 24 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 3 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 1 week

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 2 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 4 weeks

explanation.summary: The zygote divides while migrating down the fallopian tube and implants in the endometrium approximately one week after fertilization.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the two haploid gamete nuclei merge to form the zygote, it begins cell division and migrates to the uterus via the movement of cilia in the fallopian tube, implanting in the endometrium approximately one week after fertilization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Twenty-four hours describes the window after ovulation within which fertilization must occur, not the time to implantation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: At three days the dividing zygote is still in transit through the tube toward the uterine cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Two weeks overstates the interval; implantation occurs at about one week after fertilization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Four weeks is far beyond the described timeline for implantation in the endometrium.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy in the ampulla of the right fallopian tube. She asks why the tissue cannot simply be left in place. Removal of the ectopic tissue, by medication or surgery, is indicated primarily to prevent which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rupture of the fallopian tube with hemorrhage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Malignant transformation of the implanted tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ascending infection of the peritoneal cavity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of the contralateral fallopian tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progression of the fetus to term with anomalies

explanation.summary: Ectopic tissue must be removed because continued embryo growth can rupture the fallopian tube and cause life-threatening bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ectopic pregnancy is dangerous because embryo growth can result in bleeding and rupture of the fallopian tube. To prevent these life-threatening complications the ectopic tissue must be removed, either with medication that stops growth and dissolves the tissue or by laparoscopic or abdominal surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The danger of an ectopic pregnancy is mechanical rupture and bleeding, not cancerous change of the tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infection is not the described threat; hemorrhage from tubal rupture is what makes the condition life-threatening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The risk involves the tube carrying the ectopic tissue itself, not blockage of the opposite tube.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tubal pregnancy cannot safely progress; the concern is rupture of the tube as the embryo grows, not delivery of an anomalous infant.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhea and left pelvic pain has a positive serum human chorionic gonadotropin test, and ectopic pregnancy is suspected. Which of the following is used to determine the location of the pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serial serum human chorionic gonadotropin measurement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeat urine home pregnancy testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum estradiol measurement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endometrial biopsy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultrasound examination

explanation.summary: In suspected ectopic pregnancy, the hCG blood test confirms pregnancy and ultrasound examination determines its location.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ectopic pregnancy is diagnosed using the human chorionic gonadotropin blood test to confirm that a pregnancy exists, and ultrasound examination is then used to determine where the pregnancy is located, distinguishing intrauterine from ectopic implantation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: hCG testing confirms the presence of a pregnancy but does not show where the tissue has implanted.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A urine pregnancy test likewise indicates pregnancy without providing any anatomic localization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Estradiol reflects ovarian hormone production; it has no role in localizing a pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sampling the endometrium is not the described method for finding the implantation site of a suspected ectopic pregnancy.

questions.stem: In a fertilization laboratory, sperm recovered from the surface of the zona pellucida are compared with sperm remaining in the surrounding medium. The zona-bound population contains a higher proportion of capacitated sperm with better morphology and DNA integrity. This finding best reflects which of the following functions of the zona pellucida?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capture of the ovulated egg by the fimbriae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preferential selection of fertilization-competent sperm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Buffering of the acidic vaginal environment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Triggering completion of meiosis I in the oocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of lysosomal enzymes that block polyspermy

explanation.summary: The zona pellucida preferentially selects fertilization-competent, capacitated sperm and enriches for better morphology and DNA integrity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The zona pellucida, the glycoprotein layer between the corona radiata and the plasma membrane, preferentially selects fertilization-competent, capacitated sperm and enriches for sperm with better morphology and DNA integrity, which is exactly the pattern seen in the zona-bound population.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capture by the fimbriae is mediated by adhesion molecules on the corona radiata's granulosa cells, not by the zona pellucida.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vaginal acid is buffered by alkaline components of semen and cervical mucus, far upstream of the egg's layers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meiosis I is completed under the influence of the LH surge before ovulation; the zona does not drive it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysosomal enzymes that help block polyspermy come from the ovum's cortical granules, not from the zona itself.

questions.stem: During transit through the female reproductive tract, sperm undergo a biochemical change in their outer layer that enables them to fertilize an ovum. Which of the following intracellular changes mediates this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gradual fall in calcium that suppresses cAMP generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rapid efflux of potassium that raises cGMP levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: A gradual rise in sodium that suppresses cGMP levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: A gradual rise in calcium that enhances cAMP generation

choices.label: E
choices.text: A rapid influx of chloride that raises cAMP levels

explanation.summary: Capacitation is mediated by a gradual increase in intracellular calcium that enhances cAMP generation, priming sperm for the acrosome reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capacitation, which occurs in part through interaction with cervical secretions, is mediated by a gradual increase in the level of intracellular calcium, which enhances generation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate. Increased calcium and cAMP prime the sperm for the acrosome reaction that later allows penetration of the egg's outer layers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium rises rather than falls during capacitation, and cAMP generation is enhanced, not suppressed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mediator is calcium acting through cAMP, not a potassium efflux acting through cGMP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium and cGMP are not the described second-messenger pathway of capacitation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although cAMP does increase, the change that drives it is a gradual rise in intracellular calcium, not a chloride influx.

questions.stem: In an experimental fertilization system, capacitated sperm bind normally to receptors in the zona pellucida of a mature oocyte. An agent that chelates intracellular calcium within the sperm is then added. Which of the following events is most directly prevented?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Release of acrosin and other acrosomal enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of antigens from the sperm surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activation of motility in the sperm tail

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binding of the sperm to zona pellucida receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exocytosis of cortical granules by the ovum

explanation.summary: After zona binding, a calcium surge within the sperm stimulates release of acrosomal enzymes such as acrosin; blocking sperm calcium prevents this release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once binding to the zona occurs, a calcium surge within the sperm stimulates the release of acrosomal enzymes, including acrosin and other hydrolytic enzymes, which degrade the egg's layers and create a tunnel for the head, neck, and middle piece to enter. Chelating sperm calcium removes the trigger for this enzyme release.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of surface antigens is part of capacitation, which these sperm completed before binding to the zona.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tail activation also occurs during capacitation, already accomplished during transit in this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem states that binding to zona receptors proceeded normally before the chelator was added.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortical granule exocytosis is triggered by a calcium rise within the ovum after fertilization, not by calcium inside the sperm.

questions.stem: After the plasma membranes of a sperm and an oocyte fuse during fertilization, portions of the spermatozoon enter the oocyte to deliver the paternal genetic material. Which of the following describes the sperm components that enter the egg?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The head only

choices.label: B
choices.text: The head and tail only

choices.label: C
choices.text: The head, neck, and middle piece

choices.label: D
choices.text: The entire sperm including the tail

choices.label: E
choices.text: The middle piece and tail only

explanation.summary: Acrosomal enzymes create a tunnel through which the head, neck, and middle piece of the sperm enter the egg to release the genetic material.
explanation.whyCorrect: After binding, the calcium-triggered release of acrosomal enzymes degrades the egg's layers, creating a tunnel for the head, neck, and middle piece of the sperm to enter the interior of the cell and release its genetic material, after which the two haploid nuclei merge to form the zygote.

whyWrongByChoice.A: More than the head enters; the neck and middle piece accompany it into the egg.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The tail does not enter the egg, and this pairing omits the neck and middle piece that do.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The whole spermatozoon does not enter; the tail is excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The head, which carries the genetic material, is the essential entering component, and the tail stays outside.

questions.stem: A single sperm fuses with an ovum in the ampulla, while dozens of additional sperm remain bound nearby. Which of the following layers of the ovulated egg complex serves as the major defense against penetration of the egg by multiple sperm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The corona radiata

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first polar body

choices.label: C
choices.text: The oocyte cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nuclear envelope of the oocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: The zona pellucida

explanation.summary: The zona pellucida is the major defense against multiple sperm penetrating the egg.
explanation.whyCorrect: The zona pellucida, the glycoprotein layer between the corona radiata and the plasma membrane, is the major defense against multiple sperm penetrating the egg. After fertilization, cortical granule exocytosis drives changes in the structure of the zona pellucida that prevent additional sperm from binding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The corona radiata's granulosa cells aid capture by the fimbriae; hundreds of sperm can traverse this layer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first polar body is a discarded product of meiosis I; it plays no protective role against sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cytoplasm is what a penetrating sperm reaches; it is not the barrier that excludes additional sperm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nuclear envelope surrounds the oocyte's chromatin and is not a described barrier to sperm penetration.

questions.stem: A researcher compares completion of meiosis II in male and female gametogenesis. Whereas the oocyte completes meiosis II only after fertilization in the fallopian tube, spermatocytes complete meiosis II in which of the following locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the epididymis during sperm storage

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the seminiferous tubules of the testis

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the vagina shortly after ejaculation

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the uterus during capacitation

choices.label: E
choices.text: At the oolemma after membrane fusion

explanation.summary: Spermatocytes complete meiosis II within the testes, forming nearly mature sperm, whereas oocytes finish meiosis II only after fertilization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm development proceeds in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, where spermatocytes complete both meiotic divisions and form nearly mature sperm before ever leaving the male tract. In contrast, meiosis II in the oocyte begins in the ovary, halts at metaphase II, and completes only after fertilization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sperm passing through the epididymis have already completed meiosis in the seminiferous tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ejaculated sperm are post-meiotic cells; no chromosomal division occurs in the vagina.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Capacitation is a biochemical change in the sperm's outer layer during transit; it involves no meiotic division.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Completion of meiosis at the egg after fusion describes the oocyte's own meiosis II, not any division of the sperm.

questions.stem: Although the vaginal environment is acidic and toxic to sperm, a fraction of ejaculated sperm survives long enough to pass through the cervix into the uterus. Which of the following most directly provides this temporary protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolytic enzymes released from the acrosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of surface antigens during capacitation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adhesion molecules on the corona radiata

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alkaline components of semen and cervical mucus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lysosomal enzymes released from cortical granules

explanation.summary: Alkaline components of semen and cervical mucus buffer the acidic vaginal environment, temporarily protecting sperm during transit.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vaginal acidity is toxic to sperm and destroys most of them shortly after ejaculation, but alkaline components of semen and cervical mucus help buffer this environment, providing temporary protection and facilitating sperm survival as they transit into the uterus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acrosomal enzymes are released at the zona pellucida to penetrate the egg's layers; they do not neutralize vaginal acid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigen loss during capacitation facilitates binding to the egg; it confers no protection against acidity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corona radiata adhesion molecules belong to the egg and aid its capture by the fimbriae, not sperm survival in the vagina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortical granule enzymes act within the ovum after fertilization to block polyspermy; they play no role in the vagina.

questions.stem: Sperm deposited in the vagina that ultimately reach the usual site of fertilization in the ampulla of the fallopian tube must travel approximately which of the following distances?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 inch

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 inches

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 inches

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10 inches

choices.label: E
choices.text: 20 inches

explanation.summary: Transit to the ampulla of the fallopian tube requires sperm to travel a distance of about 5 inches while passing formidable barriers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transit to the ampulla, in the distal third of the fallopian tube, requires traveling a distance of about 5 inches and passing through formidable barriers, including the acidic vagina, the cervix, uterine phagocytes, and the uterotubal junction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One inch greatly understates the journey through the vagina, cervix, uterus, and tube to the ampulla.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Three inches still falls short of the roughly 5-inch distance described for transit to the ampulla.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ten inches overstates the distance from the vagina to the ampulla.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twenty inches is several times the actual distance sperm travel to the site of fertilization.

questions.stem: A couple conceives naturally after intercourse at midcycle. Which of the following correctly orders the events required for successful fertilization, from earliest to latest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ovulation, capacitation, acrosome reaction, sperm-egg fusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Capacitation, ovulation, sperm-egg fusion, acrosome reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ovulation, acrosome reaction, capacitation, sperm-egg fusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acrosome reaction, capacitation, ovulation, sperm-egg fusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Capacitation, sperm-egg fusion, ovulation, acrosome reaction

explanation.summary: Conception requires ovulation, then sperm capacitation, then the acrosome reaction, and finally entry of a single sperm into the egg.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early pregnancy depends on a series of tightly coordinated steps: ovulation releases the oocyte for capture by the fallopian tube; sperm then undergo capacitation, the biochemical maturation that enables fertilization; the acrosomal reaction follows, releasing enzymes that allow penetration of the oocyte's outer layers; and only after these steps can a single sperm enter the egg, marking fertilization.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The acrosome reaction must precede sperm-egg fusion, because its enzymes open the path through the egg's layers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Capacitation must come before the acrosome reaction; increased calcium and cAMP during capacitation prime the sperm for it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The acrosome reaction is a late event at the zona pellucida; it cannot occur before capacitation in the female tract.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fusion is the final step; it cannot precede ovulation or the acrosome reaction.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is undergoing an evaluation of ovarian steroid synthesis. In the outer cells of her ovarian follicles, luteinizing hormone binds its receptor and initiates steroidogenesis from cholesterol that has diffused in from neighboring blood vessels. Which of the following enzymes catalyzes the first step of this pathway in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aromatase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmolase

choices.label: C
choices.text: 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: 21-hydroxylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: 5-alpha-reductase

explanation.summary: In theca cells, desmolase converts cholesterol to pregnenolone, the first step toward androstenedione.
explanation.whyCorrect: Theca cells form the outer layer of the follicle and contact blood vessels, allowing cholesterol to diffuse in. After LH binds its theca-cell receptor, desmolase converts cholesterol to pregnenolone; several steps later the pathway yields androstenedione.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aromatase acts in granulosa cells, converting androstenedione to 17beta-estradiol under FSH stimulation, not in theca cells on cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase interconverts estrone and estradiol; it does not act on cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 21-hydroxylase functions in adrenal corticosteroid pathways, not in the LH-stimulated theca-cell step described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to a more potent androgen and is not the cholesterol-to-pregnenolone step.

questions.stem: Radiolabeled androstenedione is tracked within a developing ovarian follicle. It diffuses out of the cell that produced it and is converted to 17beta-estradiol in a neighboring cell. Which of the following is the cell in which this conversion occurs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theca cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulosa cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secondary oocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endometrial gland cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anterior pituitary gonadotroph

explanation.summary: Granulosa cells contain aromatase, which converts theca-derived androstenedione to 17beta-estradiol.
explanation.whyCorrect: Androstenedione made in theca cells diffuses to the more interiorly located granulosa cells. When FSH binds its granulosa-cell receptor, aromatase is induced and converts androstenedione to 17beta-estradiol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The theca cell produces androstenedione but lacks the aromatase step; the androgen leaves this cell for conversion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The oocyte is surrounded by granulosa cells but is not the site of aromatization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endometrial gland cells are hormone targets, not sites of ovarian estradiol synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gonadotrophs release LH and FSH; they do not convert androgens to estrogens.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is offered an aromatase inhibitor. He asks how his body makes estrogen when he has no ovaries. Which of the following best explains his source of estrogen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct secretion of 17beta-estradiol by the anterior pituitary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of cholesterol to estradiol in a single hepatic step

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secretion of estrone by luteinized follicular cells in the testis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of androstenedione by aromatase in adipose tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of stored estradiol from corticosteroid-binding globulin

explanation.summary: Extragonadal aromatase in tissues such as fat, bone, skin, brain, and breast converts androgens to estrogens in males.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aromatase is expressed outside the gonads, including in adipose tissue, liver, bone, skin, brain, and breast. There it converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to 17beta-estradiol, which accounts for estrogen in males and is why aromatase inhibition lowers his estrogen levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The anterior pituitary releases LH and FSH; it does not secrete estradiol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholesterol is the steroid precursor, but synthesis proceeds through pregnenolone and androgens over several steps, not one hepatic conversion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Luteinized follicular cells form the corpus luteum in the ovary; there is no such source in the testis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Binding globulins transport steroid hormones in plasma; they are not a storage source that generates estrogen.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman had her last menstrual period 6 years ago. Depletion of her ovarian follicle pool has ended cyclic ovarian activity. Which of the following is the predominant circulating estrogen in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 17beta-estradiol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Androstenedione

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pregnenolone

explanation.summary: After menopause, peripheral aromatization makes estrone the predominant circulating estrogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once the ovarian follicle pool is depleted, cyclic ovarian estradiol production ceases. Peripheral aromatization of androstenedione in extragonadal tissues becomes the main estrogen source, and estrone predominates in the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 17beta-estradiol is the principal estrogen during reproductive years, when granulosa cells produce it cyclically.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Progesterone is a progestogen, not an estrogen, and luteal production stops without ovulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Androstenedione is an androgen precursor of estrone, not an estrogen itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pregnenolone is an early steroid intermediate formed by desmolase, not a circulating estrogen.

questions.stem: In an experiment, gonadotropin-releasing hormone is administered to healthy volunteers as a continuous intravenous infusion rather than in pulses. After several days, serum LH and FSH concentrations fall. Which of the following best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased inhibin secretion from granulosa cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive feedback by estradiol on the hypothalamus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degeneration of the corpus luteum with loss of progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of the hypophyseal-portal vasculature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Downregulation of GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary

explanation.summary: GnRH must be pulsatile; continuous exposure downregulates its pituitary receptors and lowers LH and FSH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pulsatile release of hypothalamic GnRH is the basis for all reproductive hormone changes. If GnRH is delivered continuously, its receptors on the anterior pituitary are downregulated, decreasing LH and FSH secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibin selectively lowers FSH; it does not explain the fall in both gonadotropins caused by the infusion itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sustained high estradiol near the end of the follicular phase produces positive feedback and an LH surge, the opposite of the observed fall in LH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corpus luteum degeneration lowers progesterone and leads to menstruation; it does not suppress gonadotropins via GnRH exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GnRH still reaches the pituitary in this experiment; the portal route is intact and is not the mechanism of the decline.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles is studied across one cycle. For most of the follicular phase, rising estradiol suppresses gonadotropin secretion, yet at midcycle a surge of LH triggers ovulation. Which of the following best explains the surge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sustained high estradiol switches its feedback from negative to positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Falling estradiol releases the pituitary from feedback inhibition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rising progesterone from the corpus luteum stimulates gonadotrophs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activin from the ovary directly triggers a burst of LH release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibin from granulosa cells selectively augments LH secretion

explanation.summary: Near the end of the follicular phase, sustained high estradiol exerts positive feedback that produces the ovulatory LH surge.
explanation.whyCorrect: During most of the follicular phase, estradiol provides negative feedback that suppresses gonadotropin secretion. Near the end of the follicular phase, sustained high estradiol levels switch to positive feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, producing the LH surge that triggers ovulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Estradiol is high, not falling, just before the surge; the surge results from feedback reversal, not withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The corpus luteum forms after ovulation, so its progesterone cannot cause the midcycle surge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Activin promotes FSH synthesis and secretion; it is not described as triggering the LH surge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibin selectively decreases FSH secretion; it does not augment LH.

questions.stem: During the follicular phase, several follicles begin to develop, but normally only one dominant follicle matures and ovulates. A hormone secreted by granulosa cells reaches the anterior pituitary and selectively reduces the secretion of a single gonadotropin, starving less-responsive follicles of support. Which of the following is this hormone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estradiol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone

explanation.summary: Granulosa-cell inhibin selectively suppresses FSH, restricting continued maturation to the dominant follicle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhibin is secreted by granulosa cells and travels to the anterior pituitary, where it selectively provides negative feedback that decreases FSH secretion. The resulting decline in FSH stops the growth of less-responsive follicles, so a single dominant follicle matures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activin does the opposite: it promotes FSH synthesis and secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estradiol feedback suppresses gonadotropin secretion broadly during the follicular phase rather than selectively targeting FSH from granulosa cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: hCG is produced by the early embryo to rescue the corpus luteum; it plays no role in follicle selection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GnRH is the hypothalamic releasing hormone that stimulates, rather than selectively suppresses, gonadotropin secretion.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a positive pregnancy test 4 weeks after her last menstrual period. Her endometrium remains intact because the corpus luteum has continued to produce progesterone instead of degenerating. Which of the following hormones is responsible for preserving the corpus luteum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Follicle-stimulating hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Luteinizing hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibin

explanation.summary: hCG from the early embryo prevents involution of the corpus luteum, maintaining progesterone and the endometrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: When fertilization and implantation occur, the early embryo produces human chorionic gonadotropin. hCG prevents degradation (involution) of the corpus luteum, so progesterone production continues, maintaining the endometrium and the pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells during follicular development; it does not rescue the corpus luteum in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LH stimulates theca cells and surges at ovulation, but it is not the pregnancy signal that prevents luteal involution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GnRH drives pituitary LH and FSH release and is not the embryo-derived rescue signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibin selectively suppresses FSH secretion and has no role in maintaining the corpus luteum.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how 17beta-estradiol alters gene expression in breast tissue. After the hormone dissociates from its plasma carrier and diffuses across the plasma membrane, which of the following events allows it to regulate transcription of target genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hormone activates a surface G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hormone opens a ligand-gated ion channel that depolarizes the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hormone-receptor complex dimerizes and binds estrogen-response elements in DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hormone binds a receptor tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates cytosolic targets

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hormone binds ribosomes directly and accelerates translation of mRNA

explanation.summary: Estrogen binds intracellular receptors that dimerize, bind estrogen-response elements, and act as transcription factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen receptors are located primarily in the nucleus, with additional populations in the cytoplasm and at the plasma membrane. After binding, the activated receptors form a dimer that binds specific DNA sequences called estrogen-response elements, and the hormone-receptor dimer becomes a transcription factor regulating mRNA production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol is a steroid that diffuses across the membrane to intracellular receptors; its genomic action is not through cAMP-linked surface receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Steroid hormone effects develop slowly through gene transcription, unlike rapid ion-channel signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor tyrosine kinase signaling is not the described mechanism for estrogen's regulation of transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hormone-receptor complex acts on DNA to regulate transcription; it does not act directly on ribosomes.

questions.stem: A physiologist measures the distribution of progesterone in the plasma of a healthy 30-year-old woman during the luteal phase. Because the hormone is lipid-soluble and does not freely dissolve in plasma, most of it is transported bound to protein. Progesterone circulates primarily bound to which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Albumin and sex hormone-binding globulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sex hormone-binding globulin and inhibin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Corticosteroid-binding globulin and hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free hormone dissolved directly in plasma water

explanation.summary: Progesterone circulates mainly bound to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin, both made in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble and do not freely dissolve in plasma. Progesterone circulates primarily bound to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin, whereas estrogens travel mainly on albumin and sex hormone-binding globulin; these carrier proteins are synthesized in the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Albumin plus sex hormone-binding globulin is the primary carrier combination for estrogens, not progesterone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibin is a granulosa-cell hormone that suppresses FSH; it is not a plasma steroid carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin carries oxygen within red cells and is not a progesterone transport protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progesterone is lipid-soluble and cannot circulate mainly as free hormone dissolved in plasma.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman who went through menopause at age 51 sustains a vertebral compression fracture. Bone densitometry shows osteoporosis. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her bone loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased apoptosis of bone-resorbing osteoclasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess estradiol stimulating bone resorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated progesterone suppressing bone formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased apoptosis and increased activity of osteoclasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased number of bone-resorbing osteoclasts in bone

explanation.summary: Estradiol deficiency increases osteoclast number and activity, partly by decreasing osteoclast apoptosis, causing bone resorption and osteoporosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen normally increases bone mass. After menopause, loss of estradiol decreases apoptosis of osteoclasts and increases their activity, so the number and activity of bone-resorbing cells rise. The resulting increase in bone resorption substantially weakens bone and raises fracture risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol loss decreases, not increases, osteoclast apoptosis, allowing these cells to persist and resorb bone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Her estradiol is deficient after menopause; excess estradiol is not present and estrogen supports bone mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postmenopausal progesterone is low, and the brick attributes bone loss to estradiol deficiency, not progesterone excess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osteoclast numbers increase in this state; a decrease would reduce resorption rather than cause osteoporosis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman tracking her fertility notices that her basal body temperature rises by about half a degree shortly after ovulation and stays elevated for nearly two weeks. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progesterone acting on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estradiol stimulating proliferation of the endometrial lining

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibin acting on the anterior pituitary to decrease FSH

choices.label: D
choices.text: LH acting on theca cells to increase androgen synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: GnRH pulses accelerating from hypothalamic inputs

explanation.summary: Luteal-phase progesterone raises body temperature by affecting the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.
explanation.whyCorrect: After ovulation, luteal cells of the corpus luteum synthesize large amounts of progesterone. Among its functions, progesterone increases body temperature by acting on the thermoregulatory center of the hypothalamus, which explains the sustained post-ovulatory temperature rise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Estradiol's proliferative effect on the endometrium occurs before ovulation and does not raise body temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibin regulates FSH secretion and has no described thermoregulatory role.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LH-driven theca-cell androgen synthesis feeds estrogen production; it does not change the temperature set point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GnRH pulse frequency governs gonadotropin release, not the post-ovulatory temperature elevation.

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is comparing the principal naturally occurring hormones of the two classes of female sex hormones, 17beta-estradiol and progesterone. Which of the following characteristics is shared by both hormones?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are peptide hormones cleaved from a common prohormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are steroid hormones derived from cholesterol

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are amine hormones synthesized from tyrosine

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are glycoproteins composed of alpha and beta subunits

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are eicosanoids derived from membrane phospholipids

explanation.summary: 17beta-estradiol and progesterone, the principal estrogen and progestogen, are both steroid hormones derived from cholesterol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The two classes of female sex hormones are estrogens and progestogens, whose principal naturally occurring members are 17beta-estradiol and progesterone. Both are steroid hormones, and cholesterol is the precursor to all steroid hormones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither hormone is a peptide; both are lipid-soluble steroids built from cholesterol rather than cleaved from a prohormone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tyrosine-derived amines are a different hormone class; the female sex hormones are cholesterol-derived steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha and beta glycoprotein subunits describe pituitary gonadotropins, not the ovarian steroids themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eicosanoids come from membrane lipids; estradiol and progesterone come from cholesterol via the steroidogenic pathway.
