whyWrongByChoice.B: FSH and estradiol are part of the initial laboratory evaluation, but only after pregnancy has been excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TSH is also part of the step 2 laboratory panel; it does not precede the pregnancy test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imaging is used later to localize a cause (for example hematocolpos or polycystic ovaries), not as the first step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pituitary MRI is reserved for elevated prolactin, suspected pituitary disease, or visual field abnormalities.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old collegiate distance runner has had no menses for 7 months. She has lost 6 kg during the season and describes intense training and academic stress. BMI is 17 kg/m2. Pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show low estradiol with low-normal FSH and LH, normal TSH, and normal prolactin. Which of the following best explains her amenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Suppression of pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of functional ovarian follicles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolactin-mediated inhibition of gonadotropin release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scarring and obliteration of the endometrial cavity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstruction of menstrual outflow at the cervix

explanation.summary: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from suppressed GnRH pulsatility without structural disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low energy availability (low leptin), excessive exercise, weight loss, and psychological stress (high cortisol) suppress pulsatile GnRH secretion. This decreases LH and FSH release, reducing ovarian stimulation and producing low estrogen, low bone density, and loss of menstrual cycling. Her low estradiol with low-normal gonadotropins fits this hypothalamic pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicle depletion (ovarian insufficiency) produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with elevated FSH, not low-normal FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Her prolactin is normal, so prolactin-mediated GnRH suppression is excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asherman syndrome follows uterine instrumentation and leaves hormonal signaling normal; her estradiol is low.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Outflow obstruction preserves hormonal cycling and typically causes cyclic pelvic pain, which she does not have.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 8 months of amenorrhea, hot flashes, and night sweats. Pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated FSH and a low estradiol; TSH and prolactin are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Asherman syndrome

explanation.summary: Elevated FSH with low estradiol localizes amenorrhea to the ovary; before age 40 this is primary ovarian insufficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary ovarian insufficiency is loss of ovarian function before age 40, most often idiopathic, and also caused by autoimmune ovarian destruction or Turner syndrome. The pituitary appropriately increases FSH in response to failing ovaries (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), and chronic estrogen deficiency produces hot flashes, night sweats, infertility, and decreased bone mineral density.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypothalamic amenorrhea causes low or normal FSH, because the ovaries are not receiving adequate gonadotropin stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A prolactinoma would show elevated prolactin, and her prolactin is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PMOS features irregular cycles, chronic anovulation, and hyperandrogenism with normal or possibly elevated estradiol, not high FSH with vasomotor symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asherman syndrome is an endometrial problem with normal hormone levels, so FSH and estradiol would be unremarkable.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. She is short for her family and has minimal breast development. Pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show an elevated FSH and low estradiol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Karyotype analysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pituitary MRI

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum total testosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hysteroscopy

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhea with absent breast development and elevated FSH suggests congenital ovarian failure, and Turner syndrome is confirmed by karyotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Absent breast development indicates chronic estrogen deficiency, and elevated FSH localizes the problem to the ovary. Turner syndrome, an important cause of primary amenorrhea in which functional ovarian tissue is typically absent or severely impaired, is confirmed by karyotyping demonstrating 45,X or 45,X/46,XX mosaicism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pituitary MRI is indicated when prolactin is elevated, pituitary disease is suspected, or visual field defects are present; elevated FSH points away from the pituitary.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Testosterone is an additional test for suspected androgen excess (hirsutism, acne, virilization), which she does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 17-hydroxyprogesterone is likewise reserved for suspected androgen excess, not hypergonadotropic ovarian failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hysteroscopy evaluates the uterine cavity (as in intrauterine adhesions), which would not explain elevated FSH and low estradiol.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with 6 months of amenorrhea, milky nipple discharge, and frequent headaches. Pregnancy test is negative, TSH is normal, and serum prolactin is markedly elevated. MRI shows a pituitary adenoma within the sella turcica. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cabergoline

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptives

choices.label: C
choices.text: Levothyroxine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Estrogen replacement with progestin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ibuprofen

explanation.summary: Dopamine agonists are the treatment for hyperprolactinemia from a prolactinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dopamine normally exerts tonic inhibition of prolactin secretion. Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline and bromocriptine enhance this inhibition, lowering prolactin, relieving the GnRH suppression it causes, and often restoring ovulation and menstruation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hormonal contraception treats primary dysmenorrhea and regulates cycles; it does not lower prolactin or address the adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism-associated hyperprolactinemia, but her TSH is normal and a prolactinoma is present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen plus progestin is the treatment for primary ovarian insufficiency, not for a prolactin-secreting tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated menstrual pain and have no role in hyperprolactinemia.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had no menses for 5 months after a dilation and curettage for retained products of conception. Before the procedure her cycles were regular. Pregnancy test is negative, and FSH, estradiol, TSH, and prolactin are all normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her amenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intrauterine adhesions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transverse vaginal septum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hyperprolactinemia

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhea after uterine instrumentation with normal hormones is Asherman syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asherman syndrome is an acquired uterine cause of secondary amenorrhea from intrauterine adhesions and endometrial scarring, classically after uterine instrumentation in the setting of pregnancy. The adhesions and obliteration of the cavity impair normal endometrial growth and shedding, so amenorrhea occurs despite entirely normal hormonal signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ovarian insufficiency would show elevated FSH and low estradiol; her labs are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypothalamic amenorrhea requires a trigger such as weight loss, exercise, or stress, and produces low estradiol with low or normal FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A transverse vaginal septum is a congenital outflow obstruction that presents with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pain, not new amenorrhea after a procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her prolactin is normal, excluding prolactin-mediated GnRH suppression.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. Breast development and pubic hair are Tanner stage 5, and she has no cyclic pelvic pain. Pregnancy test is negative; FSH, estradiol, TSH, and prolactin are normal. Pelvic ultrasound shows normal ovaries but no identifiable uterus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mullerian agenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Imperforate hymen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Asherman syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turner syndrome

explanation.summary: Normal hormones and breast development with an absent uterus indicate Mullerian agenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mullerian agenesis may involve absence of the uterus alone or of the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. The ovaries are preserved because they develop from the genital ridges rather than the Mullerian ducts, so estrogen production, breast development, and gonadotropins are all normal. With no uterus, there is no endometrium to shed and no cyclic pain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An imperforate hymen obstructs an otherwise normal uterus, so it causes cyclic pelvic pain and hematocolpos, and the uterus is visible on ultrasound.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ovarian insufficiency shows elevated FSH and low estradiol, and the uterus is present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asherman syndrome is acquired scarring after instrumentation in a patient who previously menstruated; the uterus is present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Turner syndrome causes estrogen deficiency with delayed or incomplete puberty and elevated FSH, not Tanner 5 development with normal labs.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman reports crampy lower abdominal pain that begins with the onset of her menses, peaks during the first 24 hours, and resolves within 2 days. Symptoms began about a year after menarche, and pelvic examination is normal. Ibuprofen provides substantial relief. Which of the following sequences best explains her pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progesterone withdrawal, increased prostaglandins, uterine contractions, myometrial ischemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen withdrawal, decreased prostaglandins, uterine relaxation, endometrial atrophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolactin excess, GnRH suppression, anovulation, endometrial proliferation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prostaglandin deficiency, weak contractions, retained menstrual blood, uterine distension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progesterone excess, sustained secretory endometrium, delayed shedding, spasm of the cervix

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhea is driven by excess endometrial prostaglandin production after progesterone withdrawal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Withdrawal of progesterone after corpus luteum regression triggers endometrial breakdown. Prostaglandin production then increases, intensifying uterine contractions, decreasing uterine blood flow, and producing myometrial ischemia and pain. This mechanism is why NSAIDs work: they inhibit prostaglandin production, reducing contractions and menstrual pain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Menstrual pain follows progesterone decline with increased, not decreased, prostaglandins, and the uterus contracts rather than relaxes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prolactin excess causes amenorrhea through GnRH suppression; it is not the mechanism of cyclic menstrual cramping.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary dysmenorrhea involves prostaglandin excess with intense contractions, not deficiency with weak contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Menstruation is triggered by progesterone withdrawal, not progesterone excess with delayed shedding.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with primary dysmenorrhea is prescribed naproxen. To maximize its effectiveness, when should she begin taking the medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One to two days before her anticipated menses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after pain becomes severe

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily throughout the entire menstrual cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: On the third day of menstrual bleeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only during the week after menses ends

explanation.summary: NSAIDs for primary dysmenorrhea work best when started 1-2 days before anticipated menstruation or at symptom onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen are first-line therapy and reduce pain by decreasing prostaglandin synthesis. Starting them 1-2 days before anticipated menstruation, or at the onset of symptoms, blunts the prostaglandin surge that drives uterine contractions and ischemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Waiting for severe pain allows prostaglandin production, contractions, and ischemia to become established before the drug acts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Continuous dosing all cycle is unnecessary because the prostaglandin-driven pain occurs around menstruation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pain peaks during the first 24 hours of menses, so starting on day 3 misses the window of maximal symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The week after menses is when symptoms have already resolved; dosing then provides no benefit.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman reports 3 years of progressively worsening menstrual pain after many years of painless cycles. She also describes deep pain with intercourse and 18 months of inability to conceive. Menstrual flow is not heavy, and the uterus is normal in size on examination. Ibuprofen no longer controls her pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endometriosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary dysmenorrhea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adenomyosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uterine leiomyomas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease

explanation.summary: Progressive dysmenorrhea with dyspareunia, infertility, and poor NSAID response suggests endometriosis, the most common secondary cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus and is the most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhea. It classically produces pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility, and secondary dysmenorrhea is distinguished by later onset, progressive worsening, and poor response to initial therapy such as NSAIDs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary dysmenorrhea begins 6-12 months after menarche, is predictable with menses, has a normal exam, and responds well to NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adenomyosis (glands and stroma within the myometrium) typically causes a diffusely enlarged, painful uterus with heavy bleeding; her uterus is normal in size and flow is not heavy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leiomyomas commonly cause heavy bleeding, pelvic pressure, and uterine enlargement, none of which she has.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infectious process suggested by pelvic and cervical motion tenderness rather than years of progressive cyclic pain with infertility.

questions.stem: Four patients present with secondary amenorrhea, and each is found to have a different underlying cause. Which of the following causes places a patient at the LOWEST risk for decreased bone mineral density?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoimmune ovarian destruction

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis risk in amenorrhea comes from low estrogen; PMOS and anatomic causes do not produce estrogen deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with amenorrhea from hypothalamic, pituitary, or ovarian dysfunction are at risk for osteoporosis because of low estrogen. In PMOS, estradiol is normal or possibly elevated despite chronic anovulation, so bone density is not threatened by estrogen deficiency the way it is in the other causes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary ovarian insufficiency causes chronic estrogen deficiency, and decreased bone mineral density is an expected consequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea suppresses GnRH, lowering estrogen and bone density, as in the Female Athlete Triad.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A prolactinoma suppresses GnRH pulsatility, reducing gonadotropins and estrogen and putting bone at risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoimmune ovarian destruction is an etiology of primary ovarian insufficiency, with the same low-estrogen bone risk.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother, who is concerned that she has never menstruated. Breast development began at age 10 years, and she now has age-appropriate secondary sexual characteristics. She has no pelvic pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reassure her and reevaluate at age 15 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reassure her and reevaluate at age 16 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Begin an evaluation for primary amenorrhea now

choices.label: D
choices.text: Classify this as secondary amenorrhea and check FSH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Evaluate only if cyclic pelvic pain develops

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhea is defined as no menses by age 15 OR no menses more than 3 years after thelarche.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although she is younger than 15, thelarche occurred at age 10, and more than 3 years have now passed without menstruation. This satisfies the second definition of primary amenorrhea, so evaluation is indicated now. Thelarche confirms that estrogen exposure has occurred, making the prolonged absence of menses abnormal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Waiting until age 15 applies only when the thelarche-based criterion has not already been met; here more than 3 years have elapsed since breast development began.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Age 16 is not part of the definition; the criteria are age 15 or more than 3 years after thelarche.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary amenorrhea requires previously established menstruation, which she has never had.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cyclic pelvic pain suggests outflow obstruction but is not required before evaluating a patient who already meets criteria for primary amenorrhea.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of irregular menstrual cycles since menarche reports that her last menses was 4 months ago. A urine pregnancy test is negative. She asks whether she has secondary amenorrhea. After what total duration without menses would she meet the definition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She already meets the definition

choices.label: B
choices.text: 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: 9 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: 12 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: 24 months

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhea requires 3 or more months without menses with previously regular cycles, but 6 or more months when prior cycles were irregular.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because her cycles were previously irregular, the threshold for secondary amenorrhea is absence of menses for at least 6 months. At 4 months she does not yet meet the definition, but she will at 6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 3-month threshold applies only to individuals whose prior cycles were regular; hers were irregular.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nine months exceeds the required threshold; the definition is met at 6 months for irregular cycles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twelve months is not the defining duration for secondary amenorrhea with irregular cycles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twenty-four months is far beyond the defined threshold of 6 months.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman who is 3 months postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding has not resumed menstruating. She feels well and has no headaches or visual changes. Which of the following best explains her amenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depletion of functional ovarian follicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scarring and obliteration of the endometrial cavity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obstruction of the reproductive outflow tract

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin-mediated suppression of hypothalamic GnRH release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of ovarian tissue

explanation.summary: Lactation is a physiologic cause of amenorrhea mediated by prolactin's suppression of hypothalamic GnRH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolactin release during breastfeeding suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release, which reduces LH and FSH secretion and disrupts ovulatory cycling. This decreases, but does not eliminate, the likelihood of pregnancy, so contraception should still be discussed. Lactation, like pregnancy and menopause, is a physiologic cause that should be considered before pathologic conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Follicle depletion is the mechanism of menopause, not of postpartum lactational amenorrhea in a young woman.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometrial scarring (Asherman syndrome) follows uterine instrumentation, surgery, or infection; nothing in her course suggests it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Outflow obstruction causes cyclic pelvic pain with blood accumulation and is unrelated to breastfeeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoimmune ovarian destruction is an etiology of primary ovarian insufficiency, which would produce hot flashes and elevated FSH, not physiologic lactational amenorrhea.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman reports 10 months without menses, along with hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and decreased libido. Her cycles were regular until about 2 years ago, when they became progressively less frequent. Which of the following best explains her amenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depletion of functional ovarian follicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stress-induced suppression of pulsatile GnRH secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolactin-mediated inhibition of gonadotropin release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intrauterine adhesions from prior instrumentation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cervical stenosis obstructing menstrual outflow

explanation.summary: Menopause is a physiologic cause of amenorrhea reflecting depletion of functional ovarian follicles.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a woman in her early 50s with gradually spaced-out cycles and estrogen-deficiency symptoms such as hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and decreased libido, amenorrhea reflects menopause. Menopause is a normal physiologic process caused by depletion of functional ovarian follicles, and physiologic causes should be considered before pathologic ones.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea requires triggers such as weight loss, excessive exercise, or psychological stress, none of which are described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperprolactinemia typically presents with galactorrhea, headaches, or visual disturbances rather than classic vasomotor symptoms at the expected age of menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asherman syndrome follows uterine instrumentation, surgery, or infection and does not cause hot flashes or vaginal dryness because hormones remain normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Outflow obstruction preserves hormonal cycling and produces cyclic pelvic pain with blood accumulation, which she does not have.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia treated with an antipsychotic medication reports 5 months without menses and a milky discharge from both breasts. Pregnancy test is negative, TSH is normal, and serum prolactin is elevated. Which of the following best explains her elevated prolactin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autonomous prolactin secretion by a pituitary adenoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypothyroidism-induced stimulation of prolactin release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol-mediated suppression of pulsatile GnRH secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Depletion of ovarian follicles with loss of estradiol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blockade of dopamine's tonic inhibition of prolactin secretion

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics and other dopamine antagonists raise prolactin by removing dopamine's tonic inhibition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dopamine normally exerts tonic inhibition of prolactin secretion. Antipsychotics are dopamine antagonists, so they block this inhibition and increase prolactin levels. The elevated prolactin then suppresses hypothalamic GnRH secretion, reducing LH and FSH release and disrupting ovulation, which produces amenorrhea with galactorrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A prolactinoma is a cause of hyperprolactinemia, but a medication known to raise prolactin is the more likely explanation in a patient taking a dopamine antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypothyroidism can elevate prolactin, but her TSH is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High cortisol suppresses GnRH in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea; it does not explain an elevated prolactin with galactorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Follicle depletion causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with elevated FSH; it does not raise prolactin.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with 6 months of amenorrhea, fatigue, and galactorrhea. Pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show a moderately elevated prolactin and a markedly elevated TSH. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cabergoline therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Treatment of the underlying hypothyroidism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen replacement with progestin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptives

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nutritional rehabilitation and exercise reduction

explanation.summary: Hypothyroidism is a cause of hyperprolactinemia, and treating the underlying thyroid disorder frequently restores normal menstruation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Her markedly elevated TSH indicates hypothyroidism, which is one of the recognized causes of hyperprolactinemia. Both the elevated prolactin and the menstrual dysfunction are downstream of the thyroid disease, so management should target the underlying thyroid disorder, which frequently restores normal menstruation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline treat hyperprolactinemia from a prolactinoma; here the prolactin elevation is secondary to hypothyroidism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Estrogen plus progestin replacement is the treatment for primary ovarian insufficiency, not thyroid-related amenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hormonal contraception is used for primary dysmenorrhea and cycle regulation; it does not correct the thyroid disorder driving her amenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restoring energy balance treats functional hypothalamic amenorrhea; she has no weight loss, exercise excess, or eating disorder history.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea and monthly episodes of severe lower abdominal pain. Breast development is Tanner stage 5. On examination, the hymenal opening appears normal, but the vagina ends blindly a few centimeters from the introitus. Ultrasound shows blood accumulated in the upper vagina and uterus above an obstructing membrane in the mid-vagina. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hymenotomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cervical dilation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dopamine agonist therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical resection of the septum

choices.label: E
choices.text: NSAIDs started before each anticipated menses

explanation.summary: A transverse vaginal septum is an outflow tract obstruction treated surgically by septum resection.
explanation.whyCorrect: A blind-ending vagina with a normal hymenal opening and blood trapped above a mid-vaginal membrane indicates a transverse vaginal septum, a congenital outflow tract obstruction. Treatment of outflow tract disorders is generally surgical, and for a transverse vaginal septum the appropriate procedure is resection of the septum, which restores egress of menstrual blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hymenotomy treats an imperforate hymen; her hymenal opening is normal and the obstruction lies higher in the vagina.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical dilation is the treatment for cervical stenosis, not for a vaginal septum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopamine agonists treat hyperprolactinemia; this patient has an anatomic obstruction with preserved hormonal cycling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated menstrual pain in primary dysmenorrhea but do not relieve an anatomic obstruction.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has had no menses for 5 months following a surgical procedure on her cervix. Each month she develops several days of crampy lower pelvic pain. Pregnancy test is negative, and FSH, estradiol, TSH, and prolactin are all normal. Ultrasound shows blood distending the uterine cavity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asherman syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometriosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cervical stenosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhea with cyclic pain and hematometra after a cervical procedure indicates cervical stenosis, an acquired outflow tract obstruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cervical stenosis is an outflow tract disorder that can cause secondary amenorrhea. Because ovarian function and cyclic endometrial changes are preserved, menstrual blood is produced but cannot exit, accumulating in the uterus (hematometra) and causing cyclic pelvic pain. Treatment is cervical dilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asherman syndrome also follows uterine procedures, but its amenorrhea results from endometrial scarring that impairs endometrial growth and shedding, so blood does not accumulate and cyclic pain with hematometra is not expected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometriosis causes secondary dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility rather than amenorrhea with blood trapped in the uterine cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ovarian insufficiency would show elevated FSH and low estradiol with vasomotor symptoms; her labs are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypothalamic amenorrhea produces low estradiol with low or normal FSH and lacks cyclic pain or hematometra.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman develops amenorrhea after an endometrial infection. Pregnancy test is negative; FSH, estradiol, TSH, and prolactin are normal. She has no cyclic pelvic pain, and ultrasound shows no blood accumulation in the uterus or vagina. Intrauterine adhesions are identified. Which of the following best explains her amenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endometrial scarring impairs normal endometrial growth and shedding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obstruction traps menstrual blood within the uterine cavity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced gonadotropin secretion lowers ovarian estradiol production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility

choices.label: E
choices.text: Follicle depletion triggers a compensatory rise in FSH

explanation.summary: In Asherman syndrome, amenorrhea results from endometrial damage rather than blocked egress of blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asherman syndrome is an acquired uterine cause of secondary amenorrhea from intrauterine adhesions and endometrial scarring, which can follow uterine instrumentation, uterine surgery, or endometrial infection. Unlike outflow tract obstruction, the problem is damage to the endometrium itself with scarring or obliteration of the cavity, so normal endometrial growth and shedding cannot occur. Because little or no menstrual tissue is produced, there is no accumulated blood and no cyclic pain despite normal hormones.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Trapped menstrual blood is the mechanism of outflow tract obstruction, which causes cyclic pain and hematometra; her ultrasound shows no blood accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced gonadotropin secretion describes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, but her FSH and estradiol are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Her prolactin is normal, excluding prolactin-mediated GnRH suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Follicle depletion causes elevated FSH with low estradiol, which she does not have.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with primary ovarian insufficiency after presenting with amenorrhea, hot flashes, elevated FSH, and low estradiol. Karyotype is normal. She asks what caused her condition. Which of the following is the most common etiology of primary ovarian insufficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune ovarian destruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turner syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperprolactinemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypothyroidism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Idiopathic

explanation.summary: Primary ovarian insufficiency is most often idiopathic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary ovarian insufficiency, the loss of ovarian function before age 40, has several recognized etiologies: idiopathic (the most common), autoimmune ovarian destruction, and Turner syndrome. With a normal karyotype and no other identified cause, idiopathic disease is the most likely and most common explanation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune ovarian destruction is a recognized etiology but is not the most common cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Turner syndrome causes ovarian failure, but her normal karyotype excludes it, and it is not the most common etiology overall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperprolactinemia causes amenorrhea through GnRH suppression (hypogonadotropic), not through primary ovarian failure with elevated FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thyroid disease interferes with ovulation and menstrual regularity but is not an etiology of primary ovarian insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with primary ovarian insufficiency is started on estrogen replacement therapy, and her physician adds progestin to the regimen. Which of the following is the primary purpose of the progestin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To restore depleted ovarian follicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: To protect the endometrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: To lower circulating prolactin levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: To relieve prostaglandin-mediated cramping

choices.label: E
choices.text: To stimulate hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility

explanation.summary: In primary ovarian insufficiency, estrogen replacement is paired with progestin therapy for endometrial protection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of primary ovarian insufficiency includes estrogen replacement, progestin therapy for endometrial protection, and bone health monitoring. The progestin's role is to protect the endometrium in a patient receiving estrogen. Hormone replacement therapy is generally recommended until the age of natural menopause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No hormonal therapy restores depleted follicles; replacement addresses the consequences of low estradiol rather than reversing ovarian failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Progestin does not treat hyperprolactinemia; dopamine agonists lower prolactin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NSAIDs relieve prostaglandin-mediated menstrual pain in dysmenorrhea; that is not the purpose of progestin here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progestin is not given to stimulate GnRH secretion; the problem in ovarian insufficiency is the ovary, not the hypothalamus.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with 8 months without menses. Her cycles have been irregular since menarche, and she has hirsutism and acne. BMI is 31 kg/m2. Pregnancy test is negative and TSH is normal. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated FSH with low estradiol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low FSH with low estradiol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated prolactin with low FSH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal FSH with normal or elevated estradiol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated FSH with elevated estradiol

explanation.summary: PMOS presents with irregular cycles, chronic anovulation, and hyperandrogenism, with normal FSH and normal or possibly elevated estradiol.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irregular cycles since menarche with hirsutism and acne suggest Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), among the most common causes of secondary amenorrhea. In PMOS, estradiol is normal (or possibly elevated) with normal FSH, which distinguishes it from ovarian insufficiency and from hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction and explains why bone density is not threatened by estrogen deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: High FSH with low estradiol indicates ovarian insufficiency, which presents with hot flashes and night sweats rather than hyperandrogenism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low FSH with low estradiol indicates hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction, as in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated prolactin suggests a prolactin-related disorder, which presents with galactorrhea rather than hirsutism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated FSH reflects failing ovaries and is paired with low estradiol, not elevated estradiol.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with 7 months of amenorrhea has coarse hair growth on her chin and upper lip, severe acne, deepening of her voice, and clitoromegaly on examination. Pregnancy test is negative, and TSH, prolactin, FSH, and estradiol have been ordered. Which of the following additional tests is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Karyotype analysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pituitary MRI

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum total testosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hysteroscopy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat urine beta-hCG

explanation.summary: Signs of androgen excess direct additional testing toward androgens such as total testosterone, DHEA-S, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hirsutism, acne, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly are the characteristic physical findings of androgen excess, which can interfere with normal ovulation. Beyond the initial laboratory panel, additional studies ordered when clinically indicated include total testosterone, DHEA-S, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone; serum total testosterone is the appropriate choice among the options.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Karyotype analysis is used when Turner syndrome or another genetic cause of ovarian failure is suspected, typically with elevated FSH and absent pubertal development.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pituitary MRI is indicated for elevated prolactin, suspected pituitary disease, or visual field abnormalities, none of which are present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hysteroscopy evaluates the uterine cavity for intrauterine adhesions and would not explain virilization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pregnancy has already been excluded, and pregnancy would not cause progressive virilization.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with significant recent weight loss and academic stress has had no menses for 6 months. Pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory studies show a low estradiol with an FSH in the middle of the reference range. A student suggests that the normal FSH excludes a hypothalamic or pituitary problem. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The normal FSH localizes the problem to the ovary despite the low estradiol level

choices.label: B
choices.text: The normal FSH makes an anatomic outflow tract obstruction the most likely cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: The normal FSH with a low estradiol is diagnostic of PMOS in this patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: The normal FSH excludes any abnormality of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The FSH is inappropriately normal for the low estradiol, indicating hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction

explanation.summary: A low or inappropriately normal FSH in the setting of low estrogen points to a hypothalamic-pituitary cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: When estradiol is low, a normally functioning hypothalamic-pituitary axis should increase FSH secretion. An FSH that remains in the normal range despite low estradiol is therefore inappropriately normal and indicates hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, as in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea triggered by weight loss and stress.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ovarian cause produces an elevated FSH, because the pituitary appropriately increases FSH output in response to failing ovaries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Outflow tract abnormalities present with normal estradiol and normal FSH, often with cyclic pelvic pain; her estradiol is low.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PMOS features normal FSH with normal or possibly elevated estradiol, not low estradiol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The combination of low estradiol with a non-elevated FSH is itself evidence of HPO axis dysfunction, not of a normal axis.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with 7 months of amenorrhea and persistent headaches. She reports bumping into objects at the edges of her vision, and confrontation testing confirms visual field deficits. Pregnancy test is negative and serum prolactin is elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Head MRI

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pelvic ultrasound

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotype analysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hysteroscopy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum total testosterone

explanation.summary: Elevated prolactin, suspected pituitary disease, or visual field abnormalities are indications for pituitary imaging.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has two indications for head MRI: an elevated prolactin, possibly from a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma, and visual field abnormalities, which occur when a sellar mass compresses the optic chiasm. Persistent headaches further suggest a pituitary lesion producing mass effect, and MRI can identify a prolactinoma or other mass within the sella turcica.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pelvic ultrasound identifies outflow obstruction, uterine abnormalities, or ovarian findings; her presentation points to the sella, not the pelvis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotype analysis is used for suspected Turner syndrome with hypergonadotropic ovarian failure, not for hyperprolactinemia with visual deficits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hysteroscopy assesses intrauterine adhesions, which do not cause headaches, visual deficits, or elevated prolactin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone is an additional test for signs of androgen excess, which she does not have.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for 9 months of amenorrhea and night sweats has a negative pregnancy test. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus and small ovaries with absent follicles. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal FSH with normal estradiol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low FSH with low estradiol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated FSH with low estradiol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal FSH with elevated estradiol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low FSH with elevated estradiol

explanation.summary: Small ovaries with absent follicles on ultrasound indicate primary ovarian insufficiency, which produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
explanation.whyCorrect: On pelvic ultrasound, small ovaries with absent follicles indicate primary ovarian insufficiency. Because the ovaries cannot produce adequate estrogen despite stimulation, the pituitary appropriately increases FSH secretion, yielding an elevated FSH with low estradiol. Her night sweats reflect the accompanying estrogen deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normal FSH with normal estradiol suggests an outflow tract abnormality, Mullerian agenesis, or PMOS, none of which explains absent ovarian follicles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low FSH with low estradiol indicates hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction with understimulated but structurally intact ovaries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal FSH with possibly elevated estradiol is the pattern of PMOS, in which ovaries appear polycystic rather than small and follicle-poor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Low FSH with elevated estradiol fits none of the described causes of amenorrhea.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old ballet dancer with 8 months of amenorrhea is found to have low estradiol with low-normal FSH, normal TSH, and normal prolactin. Pregnancy test is negative. She has lost 8 kg over the past year, trains 5 hours daily, and restricts her caloric intake. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cabergoline therapy for suspected hyperprolactinemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nutritional rehabilitation with reduction in excessive exercise

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen replacement with progestin until natural menopause

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cervical dilation to relieve outflow obstruction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Levothyroxine therapy for suspected hypothyroidism

explanation.summary: Treatment of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea focuses on restoring normal energy balance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Her weight loss, caloric restriction, and intense training with hypogonadotropic labs indicate functional hypothalamic amenorrhea. Treatment focuses on restoring normal energy balance through nutritional rehabilitation, weight restoration, reduction in excessive exercise, management of eating disorders, and psychological support, which allows pulsatile GnRH secretion and menstrual cycling to recover.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dopamine agonists treat hyperprolactinemia; her prolactin is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Estrogen-progestin replacement until the age of natural menopause is the treatment for primary ovarian insufficiency, which would show an elevated FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cervical dilation treats cervical stenosis, an outflow obstruction that causes cyclic pain with normal hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid hormone replacement is for hypothyroidism; her TSH is normal.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old competitive gymnast is evaluated for amenorrhea, and her physician is concerned about the Female Athlete Triad. Which of the following correctly lists the components of this syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galactorrhea, headaches, and visual disturbances

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hirsutism, acne, and irregular menstrual cycles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and decreased libido

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low energy availability, amenorrhea, and decreased bone density

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cyclic pelvic pain, hematocolpos, and normal breast development

explanation.summary: The Female Athlete Triad is low energy availability, amenorrhea, and decreased bone density.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Female Athlete Triad includes low energy availability (caloric expenditure exceeding intake), amenorrhea, and decreased bone density. It results from a suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis with low estrogen, driven by suppressed pulsatile GnRH secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galactorrhea, headaches, and visual disturbances are findings of hyperprolactinemia, often from a prolactinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hirsutism, acne, and irregular cycles describe hyperandrogenism, as in PMOS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and decreased libido are symptoms of estrogen deficiency but are not the defined triad.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cyclic pelvic pain, hematocolpos, and normal breast development describe an outflow tract obstruction.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with an eating disorder and severe caloric restriction has had no menses for 6 months. Laboratory studies confirm hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Which of the following pairs of hormonal changes best explains the suppression of her GnRH secretion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased leptin and increased cortisol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased leptin and decreased cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased prolactin and increased TSH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased estradiol and decreased FSH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased prolactin and decreased TSH

explanation.summary: In functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, low leptin and high cortisol suppress pulsatile GnRH secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low energy availability lowers leptin, and psychological stress raises cortisol. Decreased leptin or increased cortisol suppresses pulsatile GnRH secretion, which decreases LH and FSH release. The reduced ovarian stimulation produces low estrogen levels, low bone density, and loss of normal menstrual cycling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The changes are the reverse: leptin falls with low energy availability and cortisol rises with stress.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prolactin excess, not deficiency, disrupts GnRH secretion, and TSH changes reflect thyroid disease rather than energy balance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estradiol falls, rather than rises, in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, as a consequence of reduced gonadotropin stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her hyperprolactinemia-free presentation and the energy-deficit mechanism make prolactin and TSH shifts irrelevant here.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl reached menarche at age 13. Her periods were painless for about the first year, but she now has crampy lower abdominal pain during the first day of each menses. Examination is normal, and there is no pain between periods. Her mother asks why the pain began only recently rather than with her first period. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endometrial glands have implanted outside the uterus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adhesions have progressively formed within the uterine cavity

choices.label: C
choices.text: An outflow tract obstruction has newly developed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endometrial prostaglandin production has permanently ceased

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ovulatory cycles have now become established

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhea typically begins 6-12 months after menarche, once ovulatory cycles become established.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary dysmenorrhea is painful menstruation without pelvic pathology and characteristically begins 6-12 months after menarche, when ovulatory cycles become established. Ovulation produces a corpus luteum whose regression withdraws progesterone, triggering endometrial breakdown with increased prostaglandin production, intensified uterine contractions, decreased uterine blood flow, and myometrial ischemia; early anovulatory cycles lack this sequence, so the first year of menses was painless.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ectopic endometrial glands and stroma describe endometriosis, which causes progressive secondary dysmenorrhea, typically with dyspareunia or infertility, later in reproductive life.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrauterine adhesions cause secondary amenorrhea after instrumentation or infection, not new cyclic pain in a menstruating teen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An outflow obstruction produces amenorrhea with cyclic pain and blood accumulation; she is menstruating normally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin production increases, rather than ceases, at menstruation and is the driver of her new pain.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with primary dysmenorrhea has only partial relief with appropriately timed naproxen, and she also desires contraception. Her physician prescribes a combined oral contraceptive. Which of the following best explains how this therapy reduces her menstrual pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced dopamine-mediated inhibition of prolactin secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased pulsatile GnRH release from the hypothalamus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Suppression of ovulation with reduced endometrial prostaglandin production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stimulation of endometrial prostaglandin release during menses

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intensification of uterine contractions to speed endometrial shedding

explanation.summary: Hormonal contraception treats primary dysmenorrhea by suppressing ovulation and reducing endometrial prostaglandin production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hormonal therapy is appropriate when NSAIDs are ineffective, symptoms are severe, or contraception is desired — all considerations here. Combined oral contraceptives, the patch, the vaginal ring, and progestin-containing methods suppress ovulation and reduce endometrial prostaglandin production, interrupting the prostaglandin-driven contractions and ischemia that cause the pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enhancing dopamine's inhibition of prolactin is the mechanism of dopamine agonists used for hyperprolactinemia, not of contraceptives for dysmenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Contraceptives do not act by increasing GnRH pulsatility, and GnRH changes are not the mechanism of menstrual pain relief.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stimulating prostaglandin release would worsen, not relieve, dysmenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intensified uterine contractions decrease uterine blood flow and cause ischemic pain, the opposite of the therapeutic goal.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman reports several years of progressively worsening menstrual pain and increasingly heavy menstrual bleeding. On bimanual examination, the uterus is diffusely enlarged and tender, without discrete masses. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endometriosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adenomyosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Uterine leiomyomas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary dysmenorrhea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis causes a diffusely enlarged, painful uterus with heavy menstrual bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the uterine myometrium. It is a cause of secondary dysmenorrhea and classically produces a diffusely enlarged, painful uterus with heavy menstrual bleeding, matching her progressive pain, heavy flow, and diffuse tender uterine enlargement without discrete masses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endometriosis involves glands and stroma outside the uterus, causing pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility with a uterus that is not diffusely enlarged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leiomyomas are discrete benign smooth muscle tumors; they enlarge the uterus but as distinct masses rather than diffuse symmetric enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary dysmenorrhea begins soon after menarche and has a normal examination, not an enlarged tender uterus in the fifth decade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease is suggested by pelvic tenderness with cervical motion tenderness in an infectious context, not years of progressive bleeding and uterine enlargement.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding, worsening menstrual pain, and a sensation of pelvic pressure. Bimanual examination shows an enlarged uterus. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates multiple well-circumscribed masses within the myometrium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenomyosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometriosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Asherman syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uterine leiomyomas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome

explanation.summary: Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium causing heavy bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, and uterine enlargement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium and a cause of secondary dysmenorrhea. They commonly produce heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, and uterine enlargement, and pelvic ultrasound — the preferred initial imaging study for suspected secondary dysmenorrhea — identifies them as discrete myometrial masses. Management may be medical or surgical.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenomyosis enlarges the uterus diffusely from glands and stroma within the myometrium, rather than forming discrete circumscribed masses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus and does not produce myometrial masses with uterine enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asherman syndrome is intrauterine adhesions causing secondary amenorrhea, not heavy bleeding with a mass-filled uterus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PMOS causes irregular cycles, chronic anovulation, and hyperandrogenism with polycystic ovaries, not myometrial tumors.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has 2 years of progressively worsening menstrual pain, deep dyspareunia, and 1 year of infertility. NSAIDs no longer control her pain. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus and normal ovaries. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endometriosis remains likely despite the normal ultrasound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometriosis is excluded by the normal ultrasound

choices.label: C
choices.text: The presentation is explained by primary dysmenorrhea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adenomyosis is the most likely underlying cause

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease is the most likely underlying cause

explanation.summary: A normal pelvic ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Her progressive pain, dyspareunia, infertility, and poor NSAID response are classic features of secondary dysmenorrhea from endometriosis, its most common cause. Pelvic ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging study and may suggest endometriosis or identify an endometrioma, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude the disease, so endometriosis remains the leading diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ultrasound may miss endometriosis; normal imaging cannot rule it out.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary dysmenorrhea begins soon after menarche with predictable symptoms, a normal examination, and a good NSAID response — not progressive pain with dyspareunia and infertility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenomyosis typically causes a diffusely enlarged, painful uterus with heavy bleeding, and her uterus is normal on imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease presents with pelvic tenderness and cervical motion tenderness rather than years of progressive cyclic pain with infertility.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician after her mother notices breast budding and a recent increase in her height velocity. She has no other complaints, and her examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which of the following events most likely initiated this patient's pubertal development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autonomous secretion of estradiol by an ovarian follicle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continuous, nonpulsatile secretion of GnRH from the hypothalamus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reactivation of pulsatile GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maturational increase in adrenal DHEAS production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor 1

explanation.summary: Puberty begins with reactivation of pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gonadarche is initiated when pulsatile GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus resumes, stimulating anterior-pituitary LH and FSH release. The gonadotropins then activate ovarian estradiol production, which drives breast development and contributes to the growth spurt.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autonomous ovarian estradiol secretion causes peripheral (GnRH-independent) precocious puberty, not normally timed puberty in an 11-year-old.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuous GnRH exposure desensitizes gonadotropes and suppresses LH and FSH; physiologic puberty requires pulsatile secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rising adrenal DHEAS defines adrenarche, which contributes to pubic hair and body odor but does not activate the HPG axis or drive breast development.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IGF-1 contributes to linear growth but is not the initiating signal for HPG-axis activation at puberty.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her parents have noticed adult-type body odor, mild acne, and a few dark pubic hairs over the past several months. She has no breast development, her growth curve is unchanged, and the remainder of her examination is normal. Increased production of which of the following hormones best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estradiol from ovarian granulosa cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: DHEAS from the adrenal zona reticularis

choices.label: C
choices.text: LH from the anterior pituitary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum

choices.label: E
choices.text: GnRH from the hypothalamus

explanation.summary: Adrenarche is a maturational rise in adrenal androgens (DHEA/DHEAS) from the zona reticularis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Body odor, sebaceous-gland activity with acne, and axillary and pubic hair reflect adrenal androgen action. Adrenarche results from maturation of the adrenal zona reticularis and occurs independently of HPG-axis activation, so breast development is absent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol drives breast development, which this girl lacks; it does not account for isolated androgenic changes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LH rises with HPG-axis activation at gonadarche; there is no evidence of gonadotropin-driven puberty here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Luteal progesterone requires ovulation and cyclic corpus luteum formation, which occur after menarche, not in this prepubertal child.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adrenarche occurs independently of GnRH; its initiating signal remains incompletely understood.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for testicular enlargement, pubic hair, and accelerated linear growth over the past year. Bone age is advanced. GnRH stimulation testing produces a pubertal, LH-predominant gonadotropin response. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ultrasonography of the testes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Computed tomography of the adrenal glands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotype analysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reassurance with reexamination in 6 months

explanation.summary: Central precocious puberty in a boy warrants brain MRI because an identifiable CNS cause is more likely in males.
explanation.whyCorrect: Testicular enlargement, advanced bone age, and a pubertal LH-predominant response to GnRH stimulation establish central (GnRH-dependent) precocious puberty. Brain MRI is particularly important in males because a central nervous system lesion, such as a hypothalamic hamartoma, tumor, prior irradiation, or inflammatory disease, is more often found than in females.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Testicular imaging targets peripheral causes such as a Leydig-cell tumor; the pubertal gonadotropin response indicates a central process with physiologic bilateral testicular growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adrenal imaging addresses peripheral, adrenal sources of androgen; gonadotropins would be suppressed in that setting rather than pubertal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotyping evaluates suspected gonadal dysgenesis or primary gonadal failure in delayed puberty, not early central puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Observation alone is inappropriate once central precocious puberty is confirmed in a young boy, given the likelihood of a CNS lesion.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with idiopathic central precocious puberty is started on a long-acting GnRH agonist. After a brief initial rise in gonadotropin levels, her LH and FSH concentrations fall and pubertal progression halts. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the therapeutic effect of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desensitization of pituitary gonadotropes by continuous receptor activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive antagonism of GnRH receptors on gonadotropes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of aromatase activity in peripheral tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of estrogen receptors in breast and bone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct inhibition of ovarian steroid-synthesis enzymes

explanation.summary: Continuous GnRH-receptor activation by a long-acting agonist desensitizes gonadotropes and suppresses LH and FSH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Physiologic GnRH signaling is pulsatile. A long-acting agonist provides continuous receptor activation, which after an initial stimulatory phase desensitizes pituitary gonadotropes and suppresses LH and FSH secretion. Treatment can later be stopped at an appropriate developmental age, allowing HPG-axis activity to resume.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The drug is an agonist, not a receptor antagonist; the initial stimulatory phase confirms receptor activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aromatase inhibition would lower estrogen synthesis peripherally but would not suppress gonadotropin secretion or explain the initial LH surge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen-receptor blockade acts downstream in target tissues and would not reduce LH and FSH concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The agonist acts at the pituitary; it does not directly inhibit ovarian steroidogenic enzymes.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated for breast development and rapid growth. Examination shows large cafe-au-lait macules with irregular borders that stop abruptly at the midline. Radiographs obtained after a minor fall show multiple expansile bone lesions consistent with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Which of the following best explains this patient's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early activation of pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germline loss of a tumor-suppressor gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exposure to exogenous estrogen-containing products

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of one X chromosome in all cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Postzygotic activating GNAS variant increasing cAMP production

explanation.summary: McCune-Albright syndrome results from a postzygotic activating GNAS variant causing constitutive Gs-alpha signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: The triad of peripheral precocious puberty, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and cafe-au-lait macules with irregular borders that often respect the midline defines McCune-Albright syndrome. A postzygotic activating GNAS variant produces constitutive Gs-alpha signaling and increased cAMP in affected tissues, driving GnRH-independent sex-steroid production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early GnRH pulsatility causes central precocious puberty, which does not produce fibrous dysplasia or midline-respecting skin macules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: McCune-Albright arises from a somatic activating variant, not germline loss of a tumor suppressor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exogenous estrogen can cause peripheral precocious puberty but would not explain the bone lesions or pigmented macules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 45,X karyotype causes Turner syndrome with ovarian dysgenesis and delayed, not precocious, puberty.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated for pubic hair, penile growth, and accelerated linear growth over 6 months. Serum testosterone is markedly elevated, LH and FSH are suppressed, and serum hCG is elevated. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the increased testosterone production in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early activation of pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation of Leydig-cell LH receptors by tumor-derived hCG

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypersecretion of LH by pituitary gonadotropes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased aromatase activity in peripheral tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excess androgen precursor output from the adrenal cortex

explanation.summary: hCG-secreting germ-cell tumors cause peripheral precocious puberty in boys by activating Leydig-cell LH receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: hCG from a germ-cell tumor activates LH receptors and stimulates Leydig-cell testosterone production independent of pulsatile GnRH. The resulting sex-steroid excess suppresses LH and FSH, producing the pattern of high testosterone with low gonadotropins and elevated hCG.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central precocious puberty produces a pubertal gonadotropin pattern, not suppressed LH and FSH with elevated hCG.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Measured LH is suppressed, excluding pituitary LH hypersecretion as the driver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased aromatization would generate estrogens from androgen precursors, not markedly elevated testosterone with high hCG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adrenal precursors such as DHEA are weak androgens; they do not explain elevated hCG or this degree of testosterone excess.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought in for breast development that began 3 months ago. Serum estradiol is markedly elevated, and LH and FSH are low and remain suppressed after GnRH stimulation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her pubertal changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic hamartoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Idiopathic early activation of the HPG axis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen-producing ovarian cyst or tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: hCG-secreting germ-cell tumor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Constitutional variation in pubertal timing

explanation.summary: High estradiol with suppressed gonadotropins indicates peripheral, GnRH-independent precocious puberty, which in girls suggests an ovarian source.
explanation.whyCorrect: In peripheral precocious puberty, sex-steroid production is independent of pulsatile GnRH, so LH and FSH are low or suppressed relative to the degree of sex-steroid exposure. In females this pattern most often reflects an estrogen-producing ovarian cyst or tumor, and treatment targets that underlying cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hypothalamic hamartoma causes central precocious puberty with a pubertal gonadotropin response to GnRH stimulation, not suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Idiopathic central precocious puberty is GnRH-dependent and would show a pubertal, LH-predominant stimulation response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: hCG-secreting tumors drive Leydig-cell testosterone production and cause precocious puberty in males, not isolated estrogen excess in a girl.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Constitutional variation alters timing of otherwise normal puberty; it does not produce estradiol excess with suppressed gonadotropins at age 6.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy who completed his growth spurt 2 years ago has grown less than 1 cm in the past year. Radiographs show near-complete fusion of the epiphyseal growth plates of the hand and wrist. Which of the following hormones is principally responsible for this radiographic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estradiol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Testosterone acting without aromatization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin-like growth factor 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Follicle-stimulating hormone

explanation.summary: Estradiol is the principal hormonal mediator of epiphyseal growth-plate maturation and fusion in both sexes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although the pubertal growth spurt reflects coordinated action of sex steroids and the growth hormone-IGF-1 axis, estradiol is the principal mediator of growth-plate maturation and fusion in both males and females. Closure of the epiphyseal plates ends longitudinal bone growth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Testosterone contributes to linear growth, but its effect on plate fusion depends on conversion to estradiol by aromatase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Growth hormone promotes linear growth during puberty; it does not mediate epiphyseal fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IGF-1 drives linear growth as part of the GH-IGF-1 axis but is not the mediator of growth-plate closure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FSH acts on the gonads to support gametogenic function; it has no direct role in growth-plate fusion.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought in because he is the shortest student in his class and has no signs of puberty. Examination shows prepubertal testes without enlargement. Bone age is delayed relative to chronologic age, and history reveals that his father also 'grew late' in high school. Physical examination and screening laboratory studies show no chronic disease. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klinefelter syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth hormone deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from a pituitary lesion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

choices.label: E
choices.text: Primary hypothyroidism with hyperprolactinemia

explanation.summary: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is a common, often familial variation in pubertal timing, especially in boys.
explanation.whyCorrect: Absence of testicular enlargement by age 14 defines delayed puberty in males, and CDGP is a common cause, particularly in boys. The family history of delayed puberty, delayed bone age, and absence of underlying disease support this diagnosis of exclusion, with spontaneous pubertal development expected. If delay causes substantial distress, a short course of low-dose testosterone may be considered.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary testicular failure with elevated gonadotropins, not a familial pattern of delayed but spontaneous puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Growth hormone deficiency is not suggested when short stature tracks with delayed bone age and there is a family history of late puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A pituitary lesion causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is pathologic and would not be expected with an otherwise normal evaluation and familial late-bloomer pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary hypothyroidism can suppress GnRH via hyperprolactinemia, but screening studies show no underlying disease in this patient.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for absence of breast development. She is well below the expected height for her family. Laboratory studies show low serum estradiol with markedly elevated LH and FSH concentrations. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 46,XX

choices.label: C
choices.text: 46,XY

choices.label: D
choices.text: 47,XXY

choices.label: E
choices.text: 47,XXX

explanation.summary: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes ovarian dysgenesis with primary hypogonadism: low estradiol and elevated LH and FSH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delayed puberty (no breast development by age 13) with low estradiol and elevated gonadotropins indicates primary hypogonadism, in which loss of sex-steroid negative feedback increases LH and FSH secretion. In a short girl, Turner syndrome with a classic 45,X karyotype causing ovarian dysgenesis is the most likely cause.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal female karyotype does not explain gonadal failure with short stature; primary ovarian dysgenesis in this setting points to Turner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 46,XY karyotype is not the classic finding in this presentation of a short girl with ovarian failure; the lecture links this picture to 45,X.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, which causes primary testicular failure in males.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 47,XXX is not the karyotype classically associated with ovarian dysgenesis and this hormone pattern.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old competitive distance runner is evaluated for minimal breast development. She trains 20 hours per week and has lost weight over the past year on a restrictive diet. Examination shows low body weight and Tanner stage 1-2 breast development. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low estradiol with elevated LH and FSH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated estradiol with suppressed LH and FSH

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal estradiol with an isolated elevation of FSH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated estradiol with elevated LH and FSH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low estradiol with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH

explanation.summary: Undernutrition and excessive exercise cause secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism: low sex steroids with low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic energy deficit from undernutrition and excessive exercise impairs hypothalamic GnRH secretion, producing secondary hypogonadism. The hallmark pattern is low estradiol with LH and FSH that are low or inappropriately normal, distinguishing it from primary gonadal failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low estradiol with elevated gonadotropins indicates primary hypogonadism, such as gonadal dysgenesis or injury, not a hypothalamic cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elevated estradiol with suppressed gonadotropins is the pattern of peripheral estrogen excess, the opposite of this energy-deficit state.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isolated FSH elevation with normal estradiol does not fit any of the described hypogonadism patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated estradiol with elevated gonadotropins suggests an activated HPG axis, not suppressed GnRH secretion.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for absent breast development. Blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and low serum estradiol. A disorder of steroidogenesis is suspected. Deficiency of which of the following enzyme activities best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 21-hydroxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aromatase

choices.label: C
choices.text: 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase

choices.label: D
choices.text: 5-alpha-reductase

choices.label: E
choices.text: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase

explanation.summary: CYP17A1 deficiency (17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase) causes delayed puberty with hypertension and hypokalemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: CYP17A1 deficiency disrupts both adrenal and gonadal steroid synthesis, decreasing sex-steroid production and causing delayed puberty. The same enzymatic block is associated with hypertension and hypokalemia, making the combination of absent pubertal development, high blood pressure, and low potassium the classic clue.
